chunks.content: Introduction Retinal vein occlusion (RVO) leads to visual loss second only to diabetic retinopathy. Its pathogenesis is mainly retinal vein stenosis or relaxation restriction, which, in turn, causes blood flow block or intravascular thrombosis. Retinal vein occlusion can be divided into central RVO (CRVO) and branch RVO (BRVO) [ ]. Worldwide, the prevalence of BRVO is approximately 0.4%, compared with 0.08% for CRVO, and is evenly distributed between men and women, with a higher risk in the elderly population [ ]. Macular oedema (MO), a leading cause of visual impairment, can occur with either CRVO or BRVO [ ]. The pathomechanism involves increased venous blood pressure and damage to the vessel wall, leading to fluid leakage [ ]. The accurate diagnosis and monitoring of RVO–MO have been revolutionised by advances in ocular imaging, particularly optical coherence tomography (OCT). Optical coherence tomography provides high-resolution, cross-sectional visualisation of retinal pathology, allowing clinicians to localise and delineate the extent of MO, detect associated features such as disorganisation of retinal inner layers (DRIL) or hyperreflective foci and objectively quantify central retinal thickness (CRT). These precise anatomical biomarkers are indispensable not only for diagnosis and treatment decisions with current therapies but also for defining the eligible patient population and treatment endpoints for emerging modalities, such as gene therapy [ – ]. Recently, research has focused on using anti-inflammatory and anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) therapeutic strategies to reduce MO and improve vision. Two established treatments are widely used in clinics: intravitreal ranibizumab (RNZ; Lucentis; Genentech, Inc., South San Francisco, CA, USA) and intravitreal dexamethasone (DEX; Ozurdex ® ; Allergan plc, Dublin, Ireland) implants, both of which have been approved for the treatment of RVO with MO in several countries [ ]. Dexamethasone sustained-release implants are coated with the Novadur ® solid polymer matrix (Allergan plc/AbbVie Inc.) containing the glucocorticoid DEX. The implant is injected into the vitreous cavity through the pars plana using a proprietary 22-gauge applicator. One study showed that DEX is present in the retina and vitreous for up to 6 months and reaches peak concentrations in the first 2 months after injection [ ]. Another study compared a 0.7-mg DEX vitreous implant, a 0.35-mg DEX implant and a sham injection for the treatment of MO secondary to BRVO and CRVO, revealing that DEX vitreous implants significantly reduced the risk of visual loss [ ]. In addition, a randomised controlled trial (RCT) of MO secondary to RVO found that a 0.7-mg DEX vitreous implant significantly improved visual acuity and anatomical outcomes in Chinese patients, and both best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) and CRT were better than sham injections within 3–4 months after a single DEX treatment [ ]. However, as a long-acting steroid preparation, DEX has some potential side effects, such as cataracts and glaucoma, which are more likely to occur at > 6 months of treatment and may require additional intraocular surgery, which can be regarded as a limitation of this treatment approach [ ]. At present, intravitreal injection of anti-VEGF, such as RNZ, bevacizumab and pegaptanib sodium, has become the main treatment for RVO complicated with MO [ , ]. However, due to its short half-life and short-acting effect, repeated injections are necessary after the effective concentration has been reduced. This not only increases the financial burden on patients but also introduces risks, such as infection and glaucoma, caused by intraocular injection [ ]. Based on the above research status, there are clearly many treatment methods for RVO complicated with MO. The most common treatment methods are intravitreal anti-VEGF drugs and intravitreal steroid drugs; however, it remains clinically challenging to determine which of these two treatment methods should be used [ ]. This is because the decision involves balancing their distinct profiles – anti-VEGF agents (e.g. RNZ) often provide rapid visual improvement but require frequent injections, whereas steroids (e.g. DEX implants) offer sustained therapy with fewer injections but carry a higher risk of elevated intraocular pressure (IOP) and cataract progression [ – ]. Ranibizumab and DEX implants are two of the more commonly used anti-VEGF and intravitreal steroid drugs, and many separate clinical trials have confirmed their effectiveness. At present, only the results of single studies comparing the two therapeutic effects are available [ – ]. This study adopts a meta-analysis method to compare the efficacy of RNZ and DEX, providing evidence-based advice for the selection of clinical treatment methods. Therefore, this study collects the published literature and quantifies the clinical effect and safety of these two treatments systematically through a meta-analysis. Data and methods Literature search Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines, the research team conducted a systematic search. The search cutoff date was 31 August 2025. During the search, subject headings and free words were combined for the queries. The search terms were as follows:

available [ – ]. This study adopts a meta-analysis method to compare the efficacy of RNZ and DEX, providing evidence-based advice for the selection of clinical treatment methods. Therefore, this study collects the published literature and quantifies the clinical effect and safety of these two treatments systematically through a meta-analysis. Data and methods Literature search Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines, the research team conducted a systematic search. The search cutoff date was 31 August 2025. During the search, subject headings and free words were combined for the queries. The search terms were as follows: (1) ‘retinal vein occlusion’ OR ‘retinal vein thrombosis’ OR ‘branch retinal vein occlusion’ OR ‘central retinal vein occlusion’; (2) ‘macular oedema’; (3) ‘intravitreal dexamethasone implant’ OR ‘dexamethasone’ OR ‘dexamethasone implant’ OR ‘Ozurdex’; and (4) ‘intravitreal ranibizumab’ OR ‘ranibizumab’ OR ‘Lucentis’. Inclusion and exclusion criteria The study type (RCT or retrospective study), participants (age and disease type), interventions (specific drugs and dosage range, such as 0.5 mg of RNZ) and outcome measures (measurement units and time points for BCVA, CRT, etc.) were further clarified. All included studies required quantitative data that could be used for meta-analysis. The inclusion criteria were as follows: (1) study type – RCT or retrospective; (2) study participants – adult patients with BRVO or CRVO complicated with MO (aged ≥ 18 years); (3) interventions – (i) RNZ group (intravitreal RNZ for patients with RVO complicated with MO) or (ii) DEX group (intravitreal DEX implants for patients with RVO complicated with MO); and (4) outcome measures – BCVA, CRT, IOP and number of injections. The exclusion criteria were as follows: (1) patients who had previously received intravitreal injection or laser therapy; (2) patients with complications introduced by other treatment methods; (3) incomplete data; (4) repeated published studies; and (5) reviews, case reports or other studies. Literature screening The literature screening and data extraction process was independently conducted by two researchers (LY and LYH). They were blinded to each other’s assessment results, meaning that they could not see each other’s decisions during the screening and evaluation process to reduce subjective bias. For consistency of the literature screening and data extraction, the inter-rater reliability, using the Kappa statistic for categorical variables (e.g. inclusion/exclusion decisions) and the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) for continuous variables (e.g. extracted means, standard deviations) were calculated. The final Kappa value was 0.85, and the ICC values were all > 0.9, indicating excellent consistency between the raters. Any disagreements were resolved through discussion and consultation with a third researcher (ZJ). Literature quality evaluation Two independent researchers assessed the risk. Risk of bias was evaluated using the Cochrane Handbook (version 5.1.0) [ ]. The literature quality was divided into three levels: Level A (completely meeting the criteria), Level B (partially meeting the criteria ) and Level C (not meeting the criteria). In case of disagreement, a third investigator was consulted to reach an agreement. For the quality evaluation of retrospective studies, the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale (NOS) [ ] was used, which is scored on three aspects: selection, comparability and exposure or outcome, with 1 point for each condition met and a total score of 9 points. Studies with scores < 5 were of low quality, and studies with scores ≥ 5 were of high quality. Statistical analysis In this study, the RevMan 5.3 statistical software package (The Cochrane Collaboration, London, UK) was used. For dichotomous data, odds ratios were used as effect measures; for continuous data, weighted mean differences (MDs) were used as effect measures, and effect sizes were presented as point estimates with their 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Heterogeneity among included studies was assessed through the heterogeneity test. The test level for meta-analysis was set at α = 0.05. Results Literature search results A total of 385 relevant articles were identified in the databases for this study. Following systematic screening, 10 eligible articles [ – ] were included for meta-analysis and systematic review (Fig. ). Basic characteristics A total of 1,274 patients with RVO complicated with MO treated with intravitreal RNZ or intravitreal DEX implants were included in 10 studies; there were 4 RCTs and 6 retrospective studies. The average age and gender of the patients in the literature were extracted, as well as the follow-up time (see Table ). The 4 RCTs included in this study were all evaluated using the risk assessment tool for bias in RCTs recommended in the Cochrane Handbook, and the quality rating of all the included literature was Level A (see Supplementary Table ). The NOS was used to evaluate the quality of the included retrospective studies, and the scores were 6–8. All the studies were of medium and high quality, which met the inclusion criteria (see Supplementary Table for details). Results of the meta-analysis Visual acuity changes Best-corrected visual acuity is

literature were extracted, as well as the follow-up time (see Table ). The 4 RCTs included in this study were all evaluated using the risk assessment tool for bias in RCTs recommended in the Cochrane Handbook, and the quality rating of all the included literature was Level A (see Supplementary Table ). The NOS was used to evaluate the quality of the included retrospective studies, and the scores were 6–8. All the studies were of medium and high quality, which met the inclusion criteria (see Supplementary Table for details). Results of the meta-analysis Visual acuity changes Best-corrected visual acuity is an important functional index used to measure the effect of vision treatment. A meta-analysis of BCVA changes in patients with CRVO and BRVO complicated with MO was performed, making comparisons with the baseline at each follow-up point. Best-corrected visual acuity in central retinal vein occlusion The results of the pooled analysis of BCVA improvement in patients with CRVO for both treatment modalities are shown in Fig. . The results show that BCVA (based on Early Treatment of Diabetic Retinopathy Study [ETDRS] letters) improved more significantly in patients receiving intravitreal RNZ than in patients with CRVO receiving an intravitreal DEX implant (MD = 4.16, 95% CI: 0.44–7.88, p = 0.03). The subgroup analysis showed that the difference between groups was statistically significant ( p < 0.001), indicating that the follow-up time was the source of heterogeneity among BCVA indicators. Specifically, there was no obvious difference in BCVA improvement between the two treatment modalities at 1 and 12 months, and there was no heterogeneity between the studies at 1 month (MD = 0.93, 95% CI: −1.92 to 3.77, p = 0.52, I ² = 0.0%). At 6 months, however, BCVA improved more in the RNZ group than in the DEX group (MD = 9.51, 95% CI: 6.20–12.82, p < 0.001). Best-corrected visual acuity in branch retinal vein occlusion The results of the pooled analysis of BCVA improvement in patients with BRVO for both treatment modalities are shown in Fig. . The pooled analysis showed that, overall, there was no significant difference in BCVA improvement between the two treatment groups for BRVO (MD = − 0.04, 95% CI: −0.15 to 0.07, p = 0.49). Subgroup analysis by time points revealed a temporal pattern; RNZ provided superior BCVA improvement in the early phases, with a statistically significant advantage at 1 month (MD = 0.10, 95% CI: 0.04–0.15, p = 0.0004) and 3 months (MD = 0.06, 95% CI: 0.00–0.11, p = 0.03). At later time points (6 and 12 months), the point estimates of the MDs favoured the DEX implant; however, these results were not statistically significant (at 6 months: MD = − 0.15, 95% CI: −0.38 to 0.07, p = 0.18; at 12 months: MD = − 0.13, 95% CI: −0.76 to 0.50, p = 0.68). It is important to note that the results at 6 and 12 months were accompanied by considerable heterogeneity ( I ² = 70% and I ² = 97%, respectively). A subsequent sensitivity analysis by Ozkaya [ ] confirmed that RNZ significantly improved BCVA in patients with BRVO. Following exclusion, the heterogeneity decreased by 4%, and the heterogeneity between groups was statistically significant ( p = 0.003), indicating that the follow-up time was the source of heterogeneity in BCVA in BRVO (see Supplementary Fig. ). Central retinal thickness changes Central retinal thickness represents anatomic changes in the fovea following treatment. In this study, a meta-analysis was performed on the CRT changes in CRVO in patients with BRVO complicated with MO compared with baseline at each follow-up node. Central retinal thickness changes in central retinal vein occlusion The pooled analysis showed that both treatments reduced CRT in patients with CRVO (Fig. ). Patients with CRVO treated with intravitreal RNZ had a greater reduction in CRT (MD = − 106.04, 95% CI: −203.12 to − 8.97, p = 0.03). Patients with CRVO in the RNZ-treated group had a more significant reduction in CRT at 6 months (MD = − 158.83, 95% CI: −270.08 to − 47.57, p = 0.005), but there was high heterogeneity between studies ( I ² = 66.0%). However, at 12 months, there was no difference in CRT reduction between the two treatment modalities (MD = − 31.75, 95% CI: −131.49 to 67.99, p = 0.53). Hoerauf’s sensitivity analysis [ ] demonstrated that RNZ significantly reduced CRT in patients with CRVO. Following exclusion, the heterogeneity decreased to 0% (see Supplementary Fig. ). Central retinal thickness changes in branch retinal vein occlusion The pooled analysis showed that both treatments reduced CRT in patients with BRVO, as shown in Fig. ; there was significant heterogeneity among studies ( I ² = 92.0%). The results showed that patients with BRVO treated with intravitreal RNZ had a significantly greater reduction in

CRT reduction between the two treatment modalities (MD = − 31.75, 95% CI: −131.49 to 67.99, p = 0.53). Hoerauf’s sensitivity analysis [ ] demonstrated that RNZ significantly reduced CRT in patients with CRVO. Following exclusion, the heterogeneity decreased to 0% (see Supplementary Fig. ). Central retinal thickness changes in branch retinal vein occlusion The pooled analysis showed that both treatments reduced CRT in patients with BRVO, as shown in Fig. ; there was significant heterogeneity among studies ( I ² = 92.0%). The results showed that patients with BRVO treated with intravitreal RNZ had a significantly greater reduction in CRT than those treated with an intravitreal DEX implant (MD = − 41.25, 95% CI: −81.44 to − 1.05, p = 0.04). The subgroup analysis showed that the differences between groups were statistically significant ( p < 0.0001), indicating that the follow-up time was the source of heterogeneity in the CRT changes. Central retinal thickness decreased more significantly in the RNZ group than in the DEX group at 3 months (MD = − 92.10, 95% CI: −123.12 to − 61.08, p < 0.001) and 6 months (MD = − 67.01, 95% CI: −113.44 to − 20.59, p = 0.005). The substantial heterogeneity observed in this analysis may be attributed to several factors, including differences in study design (RCTs vs. retrospective studies), variations in the treatment protocols (e.g. fixed dosing vs. pro re nata regimens for RNZ) and diversity in patient baseline characteristics, such as the duration of MO and the extent of ischaemia, which were not consistently reported across all included studies. Despite this heterogeneity, the direction of effect consistently favoured RNZ at the 3- and 6-month time points in the subgroup analysis. Treatment-induced intraocular pressure changes in retinal vein occlusion Increased IOP is a common adverse reaction to the treatment of retinal diseases with intravitreal DEX implants and intravitreal RNZ. Figure shows the IOP changes observed with both treatments in this study. At 1 month after initiation of treatment, MD = − 2.98, 95% CI: −5.79 to − 0.17 and p = 0.04; the IOP in the DEX group increased at 3 months (MD = − 2.00, 95% CI: −2.51 to − 1.50, p < 0.001) and 6 months (MD = − 1.04, 95% CI: −2.02 to − 0.05, p = 0.04) and was higher than in the RNZ group. The pooled results of all included studies showed that the IOP increase in the DEX group was higher than that in the RNZ group after treatment (MD = − 1.82, 95% CI: −2.51 to − 1.12, p < 0.001). A sensitivity analysis by Kaldirim [ ] showed that DEX significantly influenced IOP changes resulting from treatment in patients with RVO. Following exclusion, the heterogeneity decreased by 2%, and the heterogeneity between groups was statistically significant ( p = 0.0007), indicating that the follow-up time was the source of heterogeneity (see Supplementary Fig. ). Number of injections used during the treatment of retinal vein occlusion The number of injections required for intravitreal DEX implants and intravitreal RNZ to treat RVO has been of concern to clinicians. This study analysed the number of injections after 6 and 12 months of RVO treatment included in the articles. The RNZ group received significantly more injections than the DEX group at 6 months (MD = 1.97, 95% CI: 1.38–2.55, p < 0.001) and 12 months (MD = 2.74, 95% CI: 2.31–3.17, p < 0.001) after treatment. The number of injections was higher in the RNZ group than in the DEX group (MD = 2.45, 95% CI: 1.97–2.94, p < 0.001) (see Fig. ). The heterogeneity between groups was statistically significant ( p = 0.04), indicating that the follow-up time was the source of heterogeneity. Publication bias Publication bias analysis was conducted on the above analysis indicators, and no obvious publication bias was found (see Supplementary Figs. – for details). Discussion Ten high-quality articles were included in this study, and the results were reliable. The meta-analysis demonstrated that intravitreal RNZ provided a greater improvement in BCVA and a more significant reduction in CRT than the DEX implant in patients with RVO complicated by MO. Furthermore, postoperative follow-up revealed a higher incidence of elevated IOP in the DEX group. The meta-analysis of this study showed that intravitreal RNZ was superior to intravitreal DEX implants in improving visual acuity in patients with BRVO and CRVO complicated by MO. Specifically, for patients with CRVO, BCVA (based on ETDRS letters) improved more significantly in RNZ-treated patients at 6 months ( p < 0.001). For patients with BRVO, RNZ treatment showed a greater BCVA improvement at 1 month ( p < 0.001) and 3 months ( p = 0.03). These results are consistent with those of previous studies. For example, the BRAVO study assessed the efficacy and safety of intravitreal

the DEX group. The meta-analysis of this study showed that intravitreal RNZ was superior to intravitreal DEX implants in improving visual acuity in patients with BRVO and CRVO complicated by MO. Specifically, for patients with CRVO, BCVA (based on ETDRS letters) improved more significantly in RNZ-treated patients at 6 months ( p < 0.001). For patients with BRVO, RNZ treatment showed a greater BCVA improvement at 1 month ( p < 0.001) and 3 months ( p = 0.03). These results are consistent with those of previous studies. For example, the BRAVO study assessed the efficacy and safety of intravitreal RNZ in patients with BRVO complicated by MO and found that 55% and 61% of patients treated with 0.3- and 0.5-mg doses of RNZ achieved a 3-line visual improvement, respectively, compared with only 29% in the control group [ , ]. Anatomically, RNZ was also more effective than the DEX implant in reducing CRT. Patients with BRVO exhibited significant CRT reductions at 3 and 6 months, whereas those with CRVO showed a pronounced effect at 6 months. This suggests that the potent anti-VEGF effect of RNZ leads to a rapid and substantial resolution of MO. The GENEVA study, which compared different DEX doses with sham surgery, supports the concept that the peak effect of steroids may not match the initial powerful anti-oedematous action of anti-VEGF agents [ ]. The observed efficacy of RNZ in our analysis at 6 months, for both BRVO and CRVO, highlights its potent short-to-medium-term activity. Elevated IOP is a well-documented adverse event of intravitreal corticosteroid therapy. Our results consistently showed that IOP was significantly higher in the DEX group than in the RNZ group at 3 and 6 months post-treatment. Clinically, this IOP elevation is often short-term and manageable with topical antihypertensive medications [ , ]. However, vigilant monitoring is essential, as a small subset of patients (e.g. 1.7% in the study by Capone et al. [ ]) may require surgical intervention for glaucoma. Consequently, the safety profile of RNZ regarding IOP is more favourable, although this must be balanced against its higher injection frequency. The injection quantity of intravitreal anti-VEGF drugs and intravitreal steroid drugs for the treatment of RVO has been an ongoing matter of concern; however, related studies have relatively few analyses of the impact of injection frequency on clinical efficacy. The results of the meta-analysis of this study showed that at 6 and 12 months after the start of treatment, the number of injections in the RNZ group was significantly higher than that in the DEX group. The study by Yoon et al. [ ] evaluated the treatment of patients with RVO combined with MO using intravitreal DEX implants. During the 12-month period, 32% and 49% of the patients received one and three injections, respectively. Patients requiring three injections had a higher CRT and larger macular non-perfusion at baseline. In addition, adverse events, such as increased IOP (35%) and newly diagnosed cataracts (16%), occurred. The increased injection frequency of intravitreal RNZ may impose an economic burden and an increased risk of adverse reactions on patients. However, due to the different basic conditions of patients, the choice of treatment methods still needs to be determined based on the patients’ situations. For patients with RVO–MO who already have a high IOP or glaucoma factors, the advantages and disadvantages of the two treatments should be explained to them, and intravitreal RNZ treatment can be recommended. For patients with some economic pressure and no risk factors for glaucoma or cataracts, the advantage of an intravitreal DEX implant lies in the slow and stable release of the drug after a single injection, reducing the safety hazards and economic burden associated with frequent injections. In addition, the DEX implant has been included in the medical insurance reimbursement list for RVO–MO treatment since 2020 in China; therefore, it is a better choice for such patients [ , ]. Our findings can be contextualised by comparing them with the earlier systematic review and meta-analysis by Hu et al. [ ], which also compared intravitreal DEX implants and anti-VEGF agents for the treatment of RVO-related MO. This study, which included 5 RCTs with 873 patients published up to August 2018, concluded that there were no significant differences in BCVA and CRT between the two treatment groups at the primary endpoint, although it noted a substantial reduction in CRT favouring anti-VEGF agents in a subset of studies at 6 months [ ]. Our current meta-analysis builds upon this foundation in several critical aspects. First, we incorporated a more recent and extensive body of literature, including 10 studies (4 RCTs and 6 retrospective studies) with a total of 1,274 patients, almost doubling the sample size and enhancing the statistical power and generalisability of the conclusions. Second, although Hu et al. [ ] combined

that there were no significant differences in BCVA and CRT between the two treatment groups at the primary endpoint, although it noted a substantial reduction in CRT favouring anti-VEGF agents in a subset of studies at 6 months [ ]. Our current meta-analysis builds upon this foundation in several critical aspects. First, we incorporated a more recent and extensive body of literature, including 10 studies (4 RCTs and 6 retrospective studies) with a total of 1,274 patients, almost doubling the sample size and enhancing the statistical power and generalisability of the conclusions. Second, although Hu et al. [ ] combined different types of RVO (CRVO and BRVO) and different anti-VEGF agents, our study performed detailed subgroup analyses based on the type of occlusion (CRVO vs. BRVO) and specific time points (1, 3, 6 and 12 months), providing a more nuanced and clinically relevant understanding of the differential treatment effects over time. For example, we were able to demonstrate that RNZ was superior to DEX in improving BCVA at 6 months for CRVO and at 1 and 3 months for BRVO and in reducing CRT at 3 and 6 months for both types, findings that were not fully elucidated in the previous meta-analysis. Furthermore, our analysis provided a more comprehensive and quantitative assessment of safety outcomes. We confirmed that the DEX implant was associated with a significantly higher risk of IOP elevation, a finding consistent with that of Hu et al. [ ]. However, we also extended the safety profile comparison by quantitatively analysing the number of injections required, clearly showing that the RNZ group received considerably more injections over 6 and 12 months, which is a crucial factor for treatment burden and healthcare economics. Finally, the inclusion of non-RCT evidence (retrospective studies) in our review, although a limitation in terms of design hierarchy, allows for the incorporation of ‘real-world’ effectiveness data and longer-term outcomes, offering a complementary perspective to that of the rigorous but sometimes restrictive environment of RCTs. In summary, although the core conclusion of Hu et al. [ ] – that both modalities are effective – remains valid, our updated and more extensive analysis provides a finer-grained, temporally resolved and clinically differentiated comparison that can better inform personalised treatment decisions for patients with RVO-related MO. This study has several limitations. The results of the meta-analysis were obtained from different types of research designs, which may have led to bias. Second, a key limitation of our analysis is that most included studies did not stratify outcomes based on the ischaemic subtype of the RVO. Ischaemic status is a known prognostic factor, and the treatment response may differ between ischaemic and non-ischaemic variants. Consequently, our results represent an average effect across these subtypes. Future studies designed to compare RNZ and DEX implants should aim to provide subgroup analyses based on ischaemia to guide more personalised treatment approaches. Third, the potential influence of specific baseline clinical and OCT biomarkers on treatment response could not be assessed in this meta-analysis. Parameters such as lens status (e.g. pseudophakia) or the presence of specific OCT features, such as subretinal fluid (SRF) or DRIL, may predispose patients to a differential response to anti-VEGF therapy versus steroids. For example, patients with pseudophakia may be better candidates for steroid implants due to the eliminated risk of cataract progression. Similarly, the presence of SRF has been suggested in some studies to be associated with a more favourable response to anti-VEGF agents. However, the included studies did not provide stratified outcomes based on these parameters. Therefore, our results represent an average effect across heterogeneous patient profiles. Future studies should aim to analyse whether such biomarkers can serve as predictors for selecting the most effective initial therapy (anti-VEGF or steroid) on an individualised basis. Furthermore, due to the limitation of the follow-up time, the long-term therapeutic effects of the two treatment methods for > 1 year cannot be evaluated. Therefore, it is necessary to incorporate more high-quality, large-sample and long-term follow-up studies in the future to further confirm the value of the results established by the meta-analysis. This would assist in the rational selection of the treatment timing of intravitreal RNZ and intravitreal DEX implants in clinical practice. Although the current standard of care for RVO–MO revolves around repeated anti-VEGF injections or sustained-release steroids, the ultimate therapeutic goal remains achieving durable efficacy with a minimal treatment burden. By directly comparing the two predominant treatment modalities, this meta-analysis provides a robust clinical context for evaluating emerging therapies, notably gene therapy. The findings of this study underscore a fundamental clinical challenge: the trade-off between efficacy and treatment frequency. current standard of care for RVO–MO revolves around repeated anti-VEGF injections or sustained-release steroids, the ultimate therapeutic goal remains achieving durable efficacy with a minimal treatment burden. By directly comparing the two predominant treatment modalities, this meta-analysis provides a robust clinical context for evaluating emerging therapies, notably gene therapy. The findings of this study underscore a fundamental clinical challenge: the trade-off between efficacy and treatment frequency. Ranibizumab, although effective, requires frequent intravitreal injections to maintain its benefits, which poses a considerable burden on patients, caregivers and healthcare systems. Gene therapy approaches for retinal diseases aim to address this limitation by enabling the sustained endogenous production of anti-angiogenic proteins (e.g. anti-VEGF agents) from a single administration. The efficacy profile of RNZ established in this analysis helps to define the therapeutic benchmark that these novel gene-based treatments must meet or exceed. Furthermore, the sustained anti-inflammatory and anti-oedematous effect observed with the DEX implant, albeit with a different safety profile, provides proof of concept that long-acting therapies are viable and desirable for managing a chronic condition such as RVO–MO. This supports the development rationale for gene therapies designed for sustained expression. Therefore, the results of this meta-analysis not only inform current clinical choices between RNZ and DEX but also contribute valuable comparative data that can guide the design and evaluation of future gene therapy trials, potentially changing the long-term standard of care from chronic reinjection to a one-time treatment. Furthermore, the evolution towards targeted and personalised therapies underscores the critical importance of precise diagnostic biomarkers. The research by Iglicki et al. and other scholars has been instrumental in identifying and validating OCT-based biomarkers (e.g. DRIL and ORYD) that predict treatment response and disease progression in retinal diseases [ , , , ]. The application of these precise imaging criteria for patient selection was a foundational element in the studies we analysed. This approach ensures that the clinical outcomes compared in this meta-analysis are based on a well-defined pathological substrate. For future gene therapy trials, which require meticulous patient stratification and long-term monitoring, the reliance on such objective, quantifiable ancillary tests will be paramount to demonstrate efficacy and ensure that treatment is delivered to those with the precise pathology it aims to address. The findings of this meta-analysis hold substantial practical implications for ophthalmologists worldwide. First, this study provides a synthesised, evidence-based comparison of two fundamental treatment paradigms for RVO–MO: the potent but short-acting anti-VEGF strategy (RNZ) and the sustained-release anti-inflammatory strategy (DEX implant). For ophthalmologists in diverse healthcare settings – from high-volume centres in developed countries to resource-limited environments – this analysis offers critical insights to tailor treatment choices. The superior early visual gains with RNZ may be preferred in settings where frequent monitoring and injection are feasible. Conversely, the sustained efficacy and reduced injection frequency of the DEX implant present a valuable option for patients with limited access to frequent healthcare or those struggling with treatment adherence. This evidence is crucial for optimising individual patient care and for guiding the development of efficient, context-aware treatment protocols on a global scale. Second, by rigorously quantifying the distinct efficacy and safety profiles of each drug over time, this analysis empowers clinicians to make informed decisions and set realistic patient expectations. Understanding that RNZ may offer faster initial results, whereas DEX provides longer-lasting effects with fewer injections but a higher risk of elevated IOP, is essential for shared decision-making. Furthermore, the comprehensive safety comparison alerts clinicians to the necessary postoperative monitoring strategies for each treatment. For readers, this study delivers directly applicable evidence. It moves beyond the results of single trials to provide a consolidated, higher-level conclusion that can be immediately integrated into clinical reasoning. It addresses a common and challenging clinical dilemma with a clear, data-driven narrative, thereby fulfilling the journal’s mission to publish content that has a direct and positive impact on ophthalmic care worldwide. Conclusion Taking the current study evidence together with the results of this meta-analysis, we conclude that intravitreal RNZ is superior to DEX implants in improving BCVA and reducing CRT in patients with RVO complicated by MO. Specifically, RNZ was more effective in improving BCVA and reducing CRT in the early stages of BRVO, whereas it took longer to show efficacy in patients with CRVO. It is important to note that the long-term comparative efficacy (beyond 12 months) of intravitreal RNZ versus the DEX implant remains less defined due to the limited follow-up duration of the included studies. Future large-scale RCTs with longer follow-up periods are warranted to confirm the sustainability of these therapeutic effects and to establish optimal long-term treatment strategies for RVO-associated MO. However, both treatments have their advantages and disadvantages. For patients with RVO combined with MO treated with intravitreal RNZ, the injection frequency was higher than that of the DEX group, and the duration of

show efficacy in patients with CRVO. It is important to note that the long-term comparative efficacy (beyond 12 months) of intravitreal RNZ versus the DEX implant remains less defined due to the limited follow-up duration of the included studies. Future large-scale RCTs with longer follow-up periods are warranted to confirm the sustainability of these therapeutic effects and to establish optimal long-term treatment strategies for RVO-associated MO. However, both treatments have their advantages and disadvantages. For patients with RVO combined with MO treated with intravitreal RNZ, the injection frequency was higher than that of the DEX group, and the duration of therapeutic effect was shorter. Moreover, some of the literature indicates that its improvement in deep vascular complex blood flow is limited [ ]. By contrast, the intravitreal DEX implant requires fewer injections than intravitreal RNZ, has a longer duration of therapeutic effect [ ] and helps reduce the levels of inflammatory factors [ ]. However, it has disadvantages, such as a relatively high risk of elevated IOP, a high risk of secondary glaucoma and a slow onset, which require close attention during the clinical treatment process. For patients with RVO–MO who already have a high IOP or glaucoma factors, intravitreal RNZ treatment can be recommended. For patients with some economic pressure and no risk factors for glaucoma or cataracts, the intravitreal DEX implant reduces safety hazards and the economic burden. Therefore, in clinical practice, exploring the possibility of combined medication and providing targeted medication based on the individual conditions of patients should be the direction for future clinical research. References---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------68 Introduction Visual impairment is common post-stroke and includes loss or impairment of central and peripheral vision, eye movement disorders, visual neglect and visual perception deficits. Reported prevalence is about 75% and incidence about 60% of stroke survivors. Despite the importance of vision in daily life, visual impairment post-stroke is under-recognised and under detected/diagnosed. Provision of care for visual impairment post-stroke is ad hoc and lacking standardisation with considerable variation in diagnosis and management globally. , Visual impairment post-stroke is absent from many international guidelines for stroke care. In recent years, more research in the field of visual impairment post-stroke has reported on aspects of screening and detection, and there is growth in intervention studies and trials. However, there is no up-to-date overview of evidence of visual impairment post-stroke to provide guidance on this important function. As clinicians may benefit from a synthesis of the available research that allows evidence-based, or expert informed, guidance on post-stroke visual impairment, the European Stroke Organisation (ESO) commissioned this guideline. The intention of this guideline is to provide a useful resource for health professionals and researchers from multiple disciplines across stroke, neurology and ophthalmology, as well as policy makers, stroke survivors and care givers. Recognising that the potential scope of this guideline was broad, we chose to focus on two specific areas of clinical importance: diagnosis and management. The guideline followed best practice and adhered to the Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) of the ESO Guideline Group. , The methods used to formulate the recommendations and consensus statements are described later in the text. However, there are certain aspects of the approach that are worthy of mention early in the guideline and will be discussed here. However, there are certain aspects of the approach that are worthy of mention early in the guideline and will be discussed here. In planning the work, we were keen that we represent many of the clinical disciplines involved in managing people living with stroke and subsequent post-stroke visual impairment. In this guideline we took an inclusive approach. We defined the concept of post-stroke visual impairment as all problems in visual function that occur following a stroke, irrespective of whether ischaemic or haemorrhagic. As we focussed on both diagnosis and management of visual impairment following stroke, we did not restrict the scope to those areas where we knew we would find high-quality trials. We formulated the questions as Population, Intervention, Comparator and Outcomes (PICOs). We planned that where an evidence-based recommendation was not possible, we would provide an expert opinion taking in consideration all the available information and drawing on the experience and knowledge of the multidisciplinary writing group. For all PICO questions, we pre-specified strict inclusion criteria around study method (randomised controlled trials (RCTs) and observation cohorts), population size, duration of follow-up and study design. Anticipating that some areas may have few included studies, as a final part of the guideline writing process, we used the available evidence to select key research questions that should be a priority for future studies. Methods Composition and approval of the Module Working Group These guidelines were initiated by the ESO. One chairperson (Fiona Rowe) was selected to assemble and coordinate the Guideline Module Working Group (MWG). The final group contained ten experts and two chairpersons (Fiona Rowe and Anne Hege Aamodt). The composition of the MWG was designed to include those disciplines involved in the care of people living with post-stroke visual impairment and comprised multidisciplinary expertise from stroke medicine, neurology, neuropsychology, ophthalmology and orthoptics. Attention was given to achieving diversity in terms of sex and geography. The ESO Guideline Board and Executive Committee reviewed the intellectual and financial disclosures of all MWG members and approved the composition of the group. The full details of all MWG members and their disclosures is included in Supplemental Table 1 . Development and approval of clinical questions This guideline was prepared according to the ESO SOPs, which are based on the Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development and Evaluations (GRADE) framework. A list of abbreviations for the guideline can be found in Supplemental Table 2 . The MWG developed a list of topics and corresponding questions of greatest clinical interest. Questions were formatted using the PICO approach and reviewed by two external reviewers as well as members of the ESO Guideline board and Executive Committee (five reviewers in total). The MWG developed a list of corresponding outcomes of clinical interest. These were rated by members of the MWG as critical, important or of limited importance according to GRADE criteria. Final decision on outcomes used a Delphi approach in which the MWG voted in a closed survey to identify which outcomes were of highest priority on a 9-point scale from 1–3 ‘not important’ to 7–9 ‘critical’. Outcomes rated as ‘critical’ were chosen for each PICO. These were subsequently approved by the ESO Guidelines Board and Executive Committee. Results of the outcomes rating for each PICO question are included in the Supplemental Table 3 . Literature search For each PICO question, search terms were developed by the MWG and guideline methodologist. Where a validated search strategy was available, this was used or adapted. Where there was a relevant systematic review on the question of interest, the corresponding search strategy and results were used and updated as necessary. We found relevant systematic reviews for all PICOs and the searches for this guideline dated from their search dates. Search strategies and details of previous systematic reviews – are described in Supplemental Table 4 . The search was performed by the ESO Guideline methodologist. The following databases were searched: MEDLINE, Scopus, CINAHL and AMED from dates of prior systematic reviews (earliest January 2011) to March 2023. Reference lists of review articles, the authors’ personal reference libraries and previous guidelines were also searched for additional relevant records. Further, we noted potentially relevant ongoing studies for future reference by searching relevant trials registries such as ClinicalTrials.gov. Search results were uploaded into the web-based Covidence platform (Health Innovation, Melbourne, Australia) for assessment by the MWG. Screening was conducted in a two-step process. For each PICO two or more MWG members were assigned to independently screen initially the titles and abstracts of publications registered in Covidence and then in the second step to assess the full text of studies determined to be potentially relevant. Search results were uploaded into the web-based Covidence platform (Health Innovation, Melbourne, Australia) for assessment by the MWG. Screening was conducted in a two-step process. For each PICO two or more MWG members were assigned to independently screen initially the titles and abstracts of publications registered in Covidence and then in the second step to assess the full text of studies determined to be potentially relevant. All disagreements were resolved by a third MWG member. We prioritised RCTs but where data were limited, or RCT study design not relevant, we also considered health registry data analyses and large observational studies. We prespecified that studies would have to include information on a minimum of 20 adult (>18 years) stroke patients in order to allow some assumption on a reliable effect. The MWG decided that smaller studies should be considered proof of concept (unless sample size was formally powered by sample size calculation) and are more prone to publication bias. We considered only studies in humans. We included studies comprising non-stroke aetiologies but >50% were of stroke cause. We excluded publications with only conference abstracts available and non-English publications where translation was not possible by the MWG. The recommendations provided herein address the diagnosis and management of visual impairment across all stages of stroke presentation and follow-up (hyperacute, acute, subacute and chronic), acknowledging the evolving needs of stroke survivors throughout their care journey. Across the PICOs, we refer to vision screening and specialist visual assessment. Vision screening involves screening for visual impairment using vision checklists or more detailed vision screening proformas/tools and undertaken by any member of the stroke multi-disciplinary team. We refer to proformas (i.e. standardised forms) and tools interchangeably in PICOs 1–7. Specialist vision assessment indicates visual assessment by a member of the eye care team (e.g. ophthalmologist, orthoptist, optometrist) and/or neuropsychologist – the latter particularly for persistent visual neglect and visual perceptual disorders. Drafting of the document, revision and approval Each PICO question was addressed in distinct sections, in line with the updated ESO SOP. First, ‘Analysis of current evidence’ summarised current pathophysiological considerations followed by a summary and discussion of the results of the identified RCTs and other studies. Second, ‘Additional information’ was added when more details on the studies referred to in the first section were needed to provide information on key subgroup analyses of the included studies, on ongoing or future RCTs, and on other studies which can provide important clinical guidance on the topic. Third, a recommendation or expert consensus statement was added dependent on the level of evidence available. The completed guideline document was proofed several times by all MWG members and modified until agreement was reached on the full guideline content. The final submitted document was peer-reviewed by two external reviewers, two members of the ESO Guideline Board and one member of the Executive Committee. Results DIAGNOSIS PICO 1: For adults with visual problems due to stroke, does routine use of vision screening, compared to no routine vision screening, improve detection rate? Analysis of current evidence In this PICO we considered the outcome of vision assessment and, in particular, vision screening options to determine if their use improves detection of visual problems due to stroke. As upwards of 40% of stroke survivors with confirmed visual impairment do not, or cannot, report visual symptoms, it is important that detection of presence/absence of visual impairment for adults with stroke does not rely solely on patient-reported visual symptoms. For the purposes of this PICO, we considered any point in the stroke pathway. However, we were interested, particularly, in the hyperacute and acute settings as early vision screening is recommended in international stroke best practice statements and clinical guidelines (e.g. ICSWP 2023, NICE 2023). , We found eight studies that compared vision screening tools/tests to no routine vision screening or alternative stroke screening options ( Supplemental Table 5.1 ). – These studies had differing populations, screening tools and outcomes, and were therefore grouped by stage of stroke screening: pre-hospital and acute care. Study design was diagnostic accuracy test, cohort and cross-sectional with a median sample size of 100 (range 43–736; mean 204.1, SD 236.4). None were randomised controlled trials. Only two studies compared vision screening to no routine screening. For pre-hospital screening, two studies were identified for screening of visual impairment in stroke events in the prehospital setting. , These reported the use of BEFAST (Balance, Eyes, Face, Arm, Speech, Time) versus FAST (Face, Arm, Speech, Time) test, and V-FAST (Vision-FAST) versus National Institute of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) checklist. Six studies were identified for screening of visual impairment compared to alternative vision screening in hospitalised stroke survivors. – Vision screening was undertaken using a questionnaire; Cerebral Vision Screening Questionnaire (CVSQ), iPad applications (Visual Impairment Screening Assessment (VISA), StrokeVision, Melbourne Rapid Field-Neural (MRFn)) and paper-based screening tools (VISA, , Stroke and Vision Defect Screening Tool (SVDST)). Overall, sensitivity and specificity results were available for seven of the above studies. The majority of studies had a high risk of bias due primarily to being non-RCT design but low risk of bias on QUADAS assessment. Sensitivity and specificity for VFAST were 85 and 42% respectively. For hospital vision screening tools, averaged sensitivity and specificity were 87.3% and 81.8% respectively. – Detection rate data were available in 14 studies ( Supplemental Table 5.2 ), , , – with a median sample size of 73.5 (range 23–88,664; mean 6596.5, SD 23,623.6). Overall, detection rate of visual impairment in stroke survivors, across variable time periods of pre-hospital to chronic stroke stages was a mean of 64.6% (SD 28.8; median 70.5%, range 11.7–96.5%). Variable detection rates were due to heterogeneous study designs, populations (e.g. formal stroke screening programmes versus referrals based on clinician suspicion; general stroke cohorts versus specific stroke types or area of brain), and visual impairment differences (e.g. inclusion of any visual impairment versus specific types such as neglect or hemianopia). Additional information For this PICO, we included outcomes that were rated as critical by the writing group, including sensitivity, specificity and detection rate. We did not include outcomes of false positives, false negatives, positive and negative predictive values and units of assessment. However, these are important considerations for vision screening and information on these outcomes are reported for some diagnostic accuracy studies. When considering patient preferences and values, stroke survivors are quite likely to be willing to have early vision testing, whether screening or specialist assessment, as it is not time consuming and there is no risk involved. The use of vision screening is better to detect the presence of vision problems than without such screening. Furthermore, there is a higher likelihood of undesirable effects without early vision screening, for example, delayed diagnosis of visual impairment or misdiagnosis. This has implications for rehabilitation but in some instances also for treatment and survival. For example, where visual impairment is the only sequelae of stroke, accurate diagnosis of this, and the association of cause being shown to be stroke, is imperative to manage the underlying condition to prevent further and potentially catastrophic strokes. In reference to vision screening where a positive result may trigger a more detailed assessment (or referral for such) it is important to detect as many cases as possible with potential visual impairment in order to optimise stroke rehabilitation. This applies even if it risks unnecessary added vision testing for some. Here, sensitivity may be preferred over specificity. Screening with a formal vision screening tool/test/checklist (currently available: pre-hospital = BEFAST, V-FAST , ; in-patient/community = CVSQ, MRFn, SVDST, VISA , , – ), particularly in in-hospital settings, consistently detects more visual problems than no visual screening with high sensitivity and specificity across the range. There is a time trade-off versus precision for some. For example, checklists that are used as an adjunct to FAST (e.g. V-FAST, BEFAST) are quick to complete and, hence, are appropriate for pre-hospital and emergency room settings. However, they are targeted at assisting decision-making on stroke detection (stroke or other diagnosis) with emphasis on posterior circulation stroke. There is added importance in identifying visual impairment caused by posterior circulation stroke (because of the potential absence of other neurological sequelae) or detection of ocular stroke (central retinal artery occlusion) within 4 h of stroke onset, to facilitate access to timely thrombolysis. As a rapid checklist, they may miss a visual impairment and thus, lack precision/accuracy. Vision screening tools are distinct from rapid detection checklists so take longer to administer but provide more testing methods and greater accuracy of detection of visual impairment. BEFAST, CVSQ, SVDST, VISA and V-FAST are available free of charge for all clinical use and publicly funded research (accessible from: www.befast.org ; www.uni-saarland.de/fileadmin/upload/lehrstuhl/kerkhoff/Materialien_für_Diagnostik_Therapie/CVSQ.pdf ; www.aci.health.nsw.gov.au/networks/ophthalmology/vision-defect-in-stroke ; www.vision-research.co.uk ). The addition of vision components to pre-hospital stroke screening may improve the detection rate for FAST-negative strokes. , Further, higher detection rates can be achieved on acute stroke and rehabilitation units with more robust measures such as specialist eye examination by orthoptists/ophthalmologists. The vision screening tools were demonstrated to be feasible at various stages from prehospital to stroke unit acute care. Acceptability by staff and patients was observed with screening possible in acute settings and often within 3 days of stroke onset. PICO 2: For adults with visual problems due to stroke, does early assessment within one week of stroke admission, compared to later assessment, improve activities and quality of daily life? Analysis of current evidence In this PICO, we consider the timing of vision screening (vision screening rather than routine stroke screening) and, in particular, the impact of early (within 1 week of stroke onset) versus later vision assessment, on activities of daily life and quality of life parameters. We were interested in the acute setting as early vision screening is recommended in international stroke best practice statements and clinical guidelines (e.g. ICSWP 2023, NICE 2023). , We found no studies that directly compared early to later vision screening/assessment. Additional information We found four studies (two cohort, one cross sectional and one online questionnaire) that were relevant to the PICO topic but not completely aligned with the original question ( Supplemental Table 6.1 ). , – Of these, three were patient population studies with median sample size of 349 (range 245–1295; mean 629.7, SD 578.5). , , Median number of stroke survivors completing visual screening was 245 (range 22–1033; mean 433.3, SD 531.2). In assessing the evidence for this PICO, there are some considerations to review. For this PICO, we included those outcomes rated as critical by the writing group. We prioritised length of stay in the hospital and time to visual screening/assessment. Two studies reported length of stay in stroke survivors with visual impairment. , Averaged mean of length of stay for both studies was 49.69 days (SD 67.84). One study reported mean length of stay for stroke survivors with normal visual function of 13.5 days (SD 45.9). Overall, length of stay was significantly longer for stroke survivors who had visual impairment. However, this is impacted by other factors as length of stay is also significantly associated with greater stroke severity as indicated in these studies. Thus, a causal association cannot be implied. As stroke severity and visual problems are correlated, it cannot be followed that early assessment of vision will impact discharge. However, it may help predict earlier discharge. Further research is needed to that regard. All studies reported results relevant to time of visual screening. An epidemiology study with an aim of exploring feasibility of early visual assessment reported visual assessment within 4 days for over 70% of stroke survivors. The median for completing an initial visual screen was 3 days (IQR 2) and median for completing a full specialist visual assessment was 4 days (IQR 7). Norup et al. reported 81.8% were referred to the visual team for additional rehabilitation on average 8 days (SD 8.30) after admission. The importance of early visual assessment was confirmed in an international survey of current practice among orthoptists with typical overall follow-up of vision care being less than 3 months with 35.5% of orthoptists seeing patients within 2 weeks of stroke onset and 55.5% by 1 month post stroke. Räty et al. specifically studied occipital lobe stroke survivors with isolated visual symptoms. Only 20.8% arrived at the hospital within the 4.5 h therapeutic time window of thrombolysis. Delays were often caused by either not identifying the problem correctly or spending too long on preceding specialist examinations. This resulted in missed therapeutic opportunities to treat these stroke survivors who typically present with visual field defects. This indicates the importance of immediate recognition of visual symptoms associated with stroke and speedy referral to a stroke unit without the delay of visiting other specialists first. Overall, in most patients, early examination for visual disturbances within 1 week is possible and acceptable as examinations do not take long and have no side effects, with feasibility and acceptability of vision screening being clearly indicated. The median for early vision screening was at 3 days post stroke admission. This is also important, as visual impairments are frequent following stroke. Further, earlier recognition can expedite treatment (patching, prisms) and rehabilitation (scanning training) efforts, influence other therapies (e.g. physiotherapy, speech and language therapy) chosen and thus benefit

As there are no predictors of who will recover, the small percentage of patients with early recovery of their visual problems (within 3–4 weeks of onset) should not result in making all wait for a later assessment and treatment, potentially limiting adaptation, engagement in rehabilitation and activities of daily life for the majority with persistent visual impairment. PICO 3: For adults with visual field loss due to stroke, does identification of visual field loss by vision screening or specialist eye team, compared to routine stroke screen, improve detection rate and activities/quality of life? Analysis of current evidence In this PICO, we consider whether in adults with visual field loss due to stroke, identification of visual field loss by vision screening or specialist eye team, compared to routine stroke screen, improves detection rate, activities of daily living and quality of life. As with the other PICOs, we considered any point in the stroke pathway. However, we were interested, particularly, in the acute setting as early vision screening is recommended in many international stroke best practice statements and clinical guidelines (e.g. ICSWP 2023, NICE 2023). , We found no studies that directly compared visual field outcomes from vision screening or specialist eye team assessment compared to routine stroke screening Additional information Overall, we found 19 studies ( Supplemental Tables 7.1 and 7.2 ) that were relevant to the PICO topic but not completely aligned with the original question in that these studies reported visual symptoms related to visual field loss (but not objective measurements of visual field) or reported vision screening outcomes versus specialist eye team assessment (but not compared to routine stroke screening). , , , , , , , , , , , , – For this PICO, we included those outcomes rated as critical by the writing group. The high sensitivity of these visual field screening tools suggests that they truly reflect a patient’s visual field status. Their administration is in general easy for patients, due to their simplicity and short duration. To improve the diagnostic accuracy of identifying visual impairment in hyperacute strokes, the VISA and StrokeVision screens are supported by an education package with detailed instructions and a video guide, which provide background information about stroke mimics and an understanding of the visual system. , PreHAST and VISA are available free of charge for all clinical use and publicly funded research ( https://sjtrem.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s13049-017-0377-x ; www.vision-research.co.uk ). Regarding detection rates of visual field defects, we found 15 studies (two cross-sectional, 13 cohort) with a median sample size of 170 (range 22–1204; mean 302.8, SD 357.5 – see Supplemental Table 7.2 ). , , , , , , , , , - Detection rate of post-stroke visual field defects ranged from 18.1% to 79.0% (mean 40.4, SD 21.1, median 27.9), with variances mainly due to variation in the visual field indices, method of visual field testing used and population (any site of stroke vs occipital lobe only). In ten studies, the visual field was examined during vision specialist assessment, , , , , , , – and in five studies detection of abnormal visual fields was based on vision screening. , , , , During vision specialist assessment, visual fields were usually examined by formal perimetry (Humphrey systems, Dublin, CA, USA) for automated static perimetry or Goldmann/Octopus, Haag Streit AG, Switzerland for kinetic perimetry), but confrontation assessment, tangent screen and Amsler grid were also used. , , , , , , – During vision screening, visual fields were also assessed by formal or confrontation perimetry and iPad applications. , , , Homonymous hemianopia was the most common visual field defect across studies. Despite the clinical heterogeneity, studies included large numbers of patients and gave consistent findings across several settings. Although most of the above studies did not specifically aim to evaluate acceptability and feasibility issues, Quinn et al., Rowe et al. and Wijesundera et al. reported high acceptability of app-based visual field tests. – Rowe et al. found that 79.8% of stroke admissions were able to undergo visual assessment within 1 week after stroke onset. Pooled analysis of the above studies showed that in 90% of cases visual assessment had been performed within the first month after the acute episode, with a median of 3 days. Test duration was reasonable and there were no associated risks with either vision screening or specialist assessment. Hence early visual field testing is recommended in stroke patients, as it is fast and acceptable by both patients and clinicians and has high detection accuracy. The importance of prompt diagnosis of visual field abnormalities is that they may be the only presenting sign of posterior cerebral artery stroke. The primary striate cortex (area V1) in the occipital lobe processes only visual information. It is estimated that 90% of occipital lobe infarcts have only visual sequelae and 46% of stroke survivors with visual field loss report no visual symptoms. Consideration must also be given to whether visual field loss is monocular or binocular. Where suspicion is that of ocular stroke (central retinal artery occlusion), rapid referral for ophthalmic opinion is crucial. While fundus photography may show classic features of cherry red spot, very early fundus examination may not yet show signs of ischaemia. Here, optical coherence tomography is a vital screening assessment to detect inner retinal nerve layer hyper-reflectivity. Further, telemedicine opportunities can be explored to expedite ophthalmic consultation to confirm ocular stroke. Delayed stroke diagnosis may have serious implications not only on visual rehabilitation and quality of life, but in certain cases also on an individual’s survival should the underlying diagnosis of stroke be missed. Based on the available evidence, the consensus expert opinion is, for adults with stroke, early vision screening should be undertaken to detect visual field loss. Additional information We found a further three studies (cohort/cross-sectional) reporting interventions for homonymous visual field loss due to stroke ( Supplemental Table 12 ) with a median sample size of 294 (range 22–426; mean 247.7, SD 205.5). , , Overall, a range of interventions have been evaluated in relation to compensatory, substitutive and/or restitutive treatment options. Compensatory approaches to rehabilitation of vision loss as a result of stroke are aimed at improving the efficacy of eye movements to scan and search more effectively into the affected/blind hemifield to better detect objects and explore that spatial environment. Substitutive approaches use, for example, prisms to enable patients to become aware of otherwise unseen stimuli through prismatic image displacement and overlap into their sighted field. Restitutive theories presume an enhanced plasticity potential of the visual pathway with potential for improvement in visual field area and/or sensitivity. The current evidence suggests that compensatory interventions (specifically visual scanning/search training) have a positive and significant effect on the activities of daily living in patients with visual field loss after stroke, in line with previous systematic reviews on this subject. , Scanning/search training can start from as early as day 1 post stroke onset but is generally commenced at a time point when the stroke survivor has capacity and capability to do the training. There are a variety of free and paid-access training options available internationally. Visual scanning/search training adds significantly to the compensatory mechanisms that underpin adaptation to visual field loss, both during training in the early and the chronic stroke phase, with significant improvement often reported for visual scanning and search performance which, in turn, may underpin the significant improvements in daily activities and QoL despite no objective improvement (albeit not expected) in measurements of visual field parameters. The results further suggest that different types of compensatory scanning strategies are appropriate for different types of activities; for example, task specific to visual exploration of the environment versus specific to reading performance. There is not enough evidence that visual field substitutive/restitutive training can substantially adjust or improve the area of visual field loss and potential risk of adverse events. However, further research is required to evaluate how such interventions could improve sensitivity and discrimination awareness within the affected area of visual field loss, even though the static visual field loss itself persists. No information was reported about effect on falls rate or driving performance. There remains a need for further studies to comprehensively evaluate the effectiveness of suggested interventions for hemianopia, particularly for visual scanning/search training. To that end, we anticipate the outcomes of current trials of interventions for hemianopia (Eye movement training in visual field defect patients by using a 3D game; Reading training for people with hemianopia; Visual scanning training for loss of vision in hemianopia – SEARCH trial) (ISRCTN trial registry). However, lesser improvement with treatments initiated after the 4.5-h window highlight the critical timing for intervention effectiveness. The findings also suggest that while thrombolysis can be beneficial, its effectiveness may depend on various factors, including the specifics of the ocular stroke event and patient characteristics. While rtPA/alteplase for CRAO is reported as feasible and safe, and with improved visual function compared with non-treatment, data from RCTs with intravenous thrombolysis given within 4.5 h time window is still lacking. , To that end, we anticipate the outcomes of current trials of alteplase or tenecteplase for ocular stroke (THEIA (A Phase III Randomized, Blind, Double Dummy, Multicentred Study Assessing the Efficacy and Safety of IV Thrombolysis; Alteplase); TenCRAOS (TENecteplase in Central Retinal Artery Occlusion Study); and REVISION (Early Reperfusion Therapy With Intravenous Alteplase for Recovery of VISION in Acute Central Retinal Artery Occlusion)). – This research on the treatment of ocular stroke underscores the critical importance of timely intervention and its potential impact on activities of daily living, such as functional reading ability. This aspect of care is paramount, considering the significant apprehension people feel towards the loss of sight, which profoundly influences their quality of life and independence. The significant difference in activity of daily living outcomes between the intervention and control groups points to the efficacy of thrombolysis as a potentially superior therapeutic strategy for improving activities of daily living among ocular stroke survivors. This finding emphasises the need for clinicians to consider thrombolysis as a viable treatment option for eligible patients, potentially setting a new standard of care that prioritises functional recovery and quality of life. The willingness of stroke survivors to engage in treatment parallels the urgency observed in those with cerebral strokes, although concerns remain for those relying on a single unaffected eye, highlighting the diversity in patient perspectives and the need for personalised care strategies. Analysis of disposition among ocular stroke survivors towards intervention indicates a broad willingness comparable to that observed in brain stroke survivors, because of the inherent fear of losing sight, the most treasured of senses. , A small subset of stroke survivors, however, may decline interventions, especially those with one remaining unaffected eye. A further noteworthy consideration in the acceptance of this intervention is the occurrence of adverse events, which includes instances of intracerebral hemorrhage (1%), orolingual angioedema and systemic bleeding (up to 11%). , , These incidents are crucial for understanding patient hesitancy and weighing the benefits against potential risks: important information for discussion in requesting treatment consent. It is also important to highlight the increased risk of cerebral stroke within the short time window after CRAO with referral for appropriate cerebrovascular work-up, just as is the case for transient ischemic attack and minor stroke, as a preventative measure. The future treatment of ocular stroke will require close collaboration between family/general practitioners, primary eye care services (e.g. optometry)
