TBUT was evaluated using fluorescein dye instilled in the inferior conjunctival sac, and the interval between a complete blink and the first appearance of a dry spot on the corneal surface was recorded under slit-lamp examination. This standardized approach was selected, as it represents the most commonly accepted method for assessing tear film stability in clinical practice. A TBUT value of less than 10 s was interpreted as indicative of tear film instability. As with other assessments, TBUT was measured at T0, T1, T3, T6, and T12. To evaluate ocular surface inflammation, conjunctival hyperemia was graded using the validated Efron scale, ranging from 0 (normal) to 4 (severe redness). Grades were assigned as follows: 0 = normal, 1 = trace, 2 = mild, 3 = moderate, and 4 = severe. Each patient was evaluated at all four time points. This scale is publicly available for educational and clinical use. No copyright permission is required [ ]. Structural integrity of the optic nerve was monitored using spectral-domain Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) imaging with the Avanti system (Optovue Inc., Fremont, CA, USA). Retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) and ganglion cell complex (GCC) thickness were measured at baseline (T0), at the six-manth follow-up (T6) and at the final follow-up to detect any glaucomatous progression. Visual field testing was performed using the Humphrey automated perimeter (Carl Zeiss Meditec, Inc., Dublin, CA, USA), employing the Swedish Interactive Threshold Algorithm (SITA) Standard with the 24-2 program. These assessments were conducted at baseline, at six months and at the final follow-up (T0, T6 and T12) to monitor functional changes related to glaucoma progression. 2.5. Statistical Analysis Statistical analysis was performed using the Medcalc 20.1.4 statistical software package (MedCalc Software, Ostend, Belgium). A priori power analysis was performed to determine the necessary sample size, indicating that 28 patients were needed to complete the study in order to achieve power 80% at a 0.05 significance level with effect size at 0.23. For normally distributed repeated measures, ANOVA for repeated measures was applied, whereas the Friedman test was used for non-normally distributed repeated measures. Paired-sample t-tests were employed for comparisons between two time points. p -values < 0.05 were regarded as statistically significant. Missing data from patients who did not complete all follow-ups were excluded from the longitudinal analyses (complete-case analysis). 3. Results 3.1. Patient Demographics Out of the 45 patients initially enrolled in the study, 3 patients developed an allergic reaction to the medication and withdrew from the study and 3 lost one of their follow-ups, 39 completed the full twelve-month follow-up period. A total of 78 eyes were examined over a period of 12 months following the initiation of treatment with preservative-free travoprost. Demographic data of the patients recruited in the study are presented in . 3.2. Intraocular Pressure (IOP) A Friedman Test revealed a statistically significant reduction in IOP over time (x 2 (4) = 43, p < 0.001). Pairwise comparisons showed significant reductions in mean IOP from baseline (T0) to all subsequent visits (T1, T3, T6, and T12 p < 0.001), with no significant differences between T1, T3, and T6 ( p > 0.05), indicating a sustained IOP-lowering effect. Significant differences were also detected between T12 and T0,T1 and T3 timelines ( p < 0.01). Median baseline IOP was 18 [15, 20] mmHg, which decreased to 14 [12.8, 15] mmHg at 12 months, corresponding to a mean reduction of 4 mmHg (approximately 22.2% decrease from baseline; p < 0.001). These findings are illustrated in and . 3.3. Ocular Surface Parameters Statistical comparisons across the follow-up period demonstrated notable improvements in ocular surface health after the initiation of preservative-free travoprost. Tear production, as assessed by the Schirmer test, showed a statistically significant increase over time, with Friedman Test revealing a significant main effect (x 2 (3) = 27.4, p < 0.001). Pairwise analysis confirmed that Schirmer scores were significantly higher at all follow-up visits (T1, T3, T6 and T12) compared to baseline (T0) ( p < 0.001), and a further significant improvement was observed between T1 and T6 ( p = 0.003) and T3 and T12 ( p < 0.001). Conjunctival hyperemia also improved significantly, with a Friedman test indicating a reduction in scores over time (χ 2 (4) = 34.5, p < 0.001). Pairwise comparisons demonstrated statistically significant decreases in hyperemia from baseline to each follow-up until T6 ( p < 0.05), with additional improvements detected between T1 and T6 ( p < 0.038), between T3 and T6 ( p

all follow-up visits (T1, T3, T6 and T12) compared to baseline (T0) ( p < 0.001), and a further significant improvement was observed between T1 and T6 ( p = 0.003) and T3 and T12 ( p < 0.001). Conjunctival hyperemia also improved significantly, with a Friedman test indicating a reduction in scores over time (χ 2 (4) = 34.5, p < 0.001). Pairwise comparisons demonstrated statistically significant decreases in hyperemia from baseline to each follow-up until T6 ( p < 0.05), with additional improvements detected between T1 and T6 ( p < 0.038), between T3 and T6 ( p < 0.007), between T1 and T12 ( p = 0.003) and between T3 and T12 ( p < 0.001). In contrast, tear film stability, as measured by Tear Break-Up Time (TBUT), remained stable throughout the study period. Repeated measures ANOVA yielded no statistically significant differences in TBUT across visits (F(4) = 2.06, p = 0.1). Post hoc analysis after Bonferroni correction showed no statistical differences between each follow-up timeline. These findings are further detailed in and illustrated in , and . 3.4. Glaucoma Indices Comparative analysis between baseline (T0), the six-month follow-up (T6) and the twelve-month follow-up revealed no statistically significant deterioration in either functional or structural parameters associated with glaucoma progression. The mean change from baseline in Visual Field Index (VFI) was −1.08 ± 0.84, which did not reach statistical significance ( p = 0.218). Similarly, MD showed a minor shift of 0.141 ± 0.018 dB ( p = 0.15), while Pattern Standard Deviation (PSD) changed by 0.072 ± 0.09 dB ( p = 0.39). Structural metrics assessed via OCT also remained stable, with the RNFL decreasing from baseline by −2.5 ± 1.99 µm ( p = 0.11), and the GCC by −1.8 ± 3.72 µm ( p = 0.18). These results, presented in , indicate that treatment with preservative-free travoprost did not contribute to measurable glaucomatous progression over the twelve-month observation period. Based on the study results, it is evident that IOP is better controlled with travoprost compared to the previous treatment. Specifically, IOP values before treatment with travoprost showed a statistically significant difference compared to all values during follow-up ( p < 0.01), while no difference was observed between measurements at T1, T3, and T6 time points ( p > 0.05). The twelve-month follow-up showed significant difference between T1 and T3 follow-ups. Regarding the severity parameters of ocular surface disease, clear improvement was observed in the Schirmer test and conjunctival hyperemia, while no improvement was seen in TBUT. Schirmer test at treatment initiation showed significant difference compared to all time points (T1–T12) ( p < 0.01), with a difference also noted between T1 and T6 ( p < 0.05) and T3 and T12 ( p < 0.001). Conjunctival hyperemia improved significantly, with differences observed between baseline and all time points (T1–T12), as well as between T1 and T6, T3 and T6, T1 and T12 and T3 and T12 time points. The TBUT index showed no significant change during patients’ follow-up ( p > 0.05). As for the clinical indices of glaucoma progression during treatment, results indicate that preservative-free travoprost can effectively control glaucoma progression in patients with mild or moderate glaucoma, based on non-significant differences indicated through the follow-ups between VFI, MD, PSD, RNFL and GCC. 4. Discussion The findings of this study demonstrate that preservative-free travoprost is effective in significantly lowering IOP in patients with mild to moderate POAG, aligning with the efficacy reported in earlier clinical trials. This reinforces its potential role as a reliable first-line treatment. Crucially, the therapeutic benefits were achieved without exacerbating OSD, a common concern with preserved formulations, particularly those containing BAK. A particularly noteworthy result was the significant improvement in Schirmer test scores, suggesting enhanced tear production in patients treated with preservative-free travoprost. This is especially important for individuals predisposed to or already experiencing dry eye symptoms. The elimination of preservatives appears to minimize ocular surface stress, a theory further supported by the reduction in conjunctival hyperemia observed throughout the study. This aligns with the hypothesis that preservatives, particularly BAK, may induce low-grade inflammation and epithelial toxicity, exacerbating OSD during long-term topical therapy. The observed improvement in Schirmer test values indicates enhanced basal tear secretion, suggesting that the switch to preservative-free travoprost may help restore tear film homeostasis in patients with ocular surface compromise. This finding is clinically relevant, as increased tear production can alleviate dry eye symptoms, improve visual comfort, and support better adherence to long-term glaucoma therapy. Similarly, the significant reduction in conjunctival hyperemia reflects decreased ocular surface inflammation and irritation, both of which are frequently associated with preserved formulations. Together, these outcomes underscore the ocular surface benefits of preservative-free travoprost, contributing not only to patient tolerability but also to overall quality of life and treatment compliance. Together, these outcomes underscore the ocular surface benefits of preservative-free travoprost, contributing not only to patient tolerability but also to overall quality of life and treatment compliance. While TBUT remained unchanged, this outcome may reflect the chronic and multifactorial nature of tear film instability, which is unlikely to resolve rapidly. The lack of TBUT improvement could also be influenced by the limitations of the test itself, which primarily assesses the lipid layer rather than the mucin layer-possibly the primary site of preservative-induced damage. The concurrent improvement in hyperemia despite stable TBUT suggests that underlying mucin-related dysfunction may have improved even if not fully captured by TBUT measurements [ ]. Importantly, no statistically significant changes were observed in glaucoma indices, including VFI, MD, PSD, RNFL, GCC thickness during the 12-month follow-up period. These findings suggest that preservative-free travoprost maintained effective IOP control sufficient to preserve both structural and functional stability. Although the study duration may not have been long enough to detect subtle progressive changes, the absence of deterioration across these parameters indicates stable disease under treatment, supporting the efficacy and safety of preservative-free travoprost in maintaining glaucomatous stability. An additional aspect that warrants consideration is the cost–benefit profile of preservative-free formulations. Although preservative-free prostaglandin analogues are generally associated with higher acquisition costs compared with preserved alternatives, these expenses may be offset by potential long-term savings. Preservatives such as BAK contribute to ocular surface disease, which frequently leads to increased healthcare utilization through the need for additional lubricants, anti-inflammatory treatments, and even surgical interventions in severe cases. Moreover, ocular discomfort and intolerance can negatively affect adherence to glaucoma therapy, increasing the risk of disease progression and associated costs. In patients with pre-existing ocular surface disease, the use of preservative-free therapy may therefore not only improve comfort and adherence but also reduce secondary treatment burden and long-term expenditure. By minimizing preservative-related ocular surface complications and improving patient tolerance, preservative-free formulations may enhance both quality of life and long-term cost-effectiveness of glaucoma management. Future pharmacoeconomic studies are needed to quantify these potential savings and further inform treatment decisions [ ]. The present findings are consistent with prior studies examining preservative-free glaucoma therapies. Pisella et al. (2002), in a large observational study, found a significantly higher prevalence of OSD symptoms in patients using preserved medications [ ]. Switching to preservative-free drops led to symptom improvement in most cases. Similarly, Oddone et al. (2022) demonstrated that patients switching to preservative-free tafluprost/timolol experienced both improved IOP control and reduced OSD signs [ ]. Jandroković et al. (2022) also reported improved ocular surface integrity and reduced hyperemia following a similar therapeutic switch [ ]. Although other studies, such as those by Shedden et al. (2010) and Day et al. (2013), found comparable efficacy and tolerability between preserved and preservative-free treatments, the trend across multiple investigations supports a favorable safety profile for preservative-free agents, particularly in patients with ocular surface sensitivity [ , ]. Goldberg et al. in 2014 compared the efficacy of two bimatoprost/timolol formulations (with and without preservatives) [ ]. A total of 561 patients with primary open-angle glaucoma and ocular hypertension were randomly assigned in this study. The study results showed the non-inferiority of the preservative-free formulation compared to the preservative-containing one in IOP control, with no significant differences observed in conjunctival hyperemia and punctate keratitis [ ]. Aihara et al. (2012) provided long-term evidence for BAK-free travoprost, showing sustained IOP reduction and notable improvements in corneal and conjunctival health [ ]. Collectively, the current study adds to a growing body of evidence suggesting that while preservative-free medications perform comparably to preserved ones in IOP control, they may offer superior ocular surface tolerability. Nevertheless, discrepancies in the literature highlight the need for larger, randomized, long-term studies directly comparing these formulations under standardized conditions. Kumar et al. (2020) compared BAK-preserved travoprost with BAKfree travoprost in Indian glaucoma patients and reported that the BAC-free formulation was associated with significantly fewer ocular surface disease symptoms and better quality of life [ ]. Ruangvaravate et al. (2020) studied patients switching from other prostaglandins to tafluprost or preservative-free tafluprost and demonstrated improvements in ocular surface parameters, with the preservative-free formulation providing the greatest benefit [ ]. Muz et al. (2021) [ ] compared BAK-preserved latanoprost with polyquad-preserved travoprost and observed superior ocular surface outcomes with the polyquad-preserved formulation, while intraocular pressure reduction remained comparable between groups. (2021) [ ] compared BAK-preserved latanoprost with polyquad-preserved travoprost and observed superior ocular surface outcomes with the polyquad-preserved formulation, while intraocular pressure reduction remained comparable between groups. These findings are consistent with the present study, which further extends the literature by specifically evaluating a completely preservative-free travoprost formulation. Unlike formulations containing alternative preservatives such as polyquad, our results suggest that the elimination of all preservatives may provide additional advantages for ocular surface health, while maintaining robust efficacy in IOP control [ , , ]. As mentioned above, our findings are consistent with yet expand upon, the growing body of evidence supporting the efficacy and tolerability of preservative-free prostaglandin analogues. Early studies, such as those by Pisella et al. (2002), demonstrated significant improvement in ocular surface symptoms following a switch from preserved to preservative-free glaucoma medications, while Oddone et al. (2022) and Jandroković et al. (2022) further confirmed improvements in ocular surface integrity and reduction in hyperemia with preservative-free tafluprost/timolol combinations [ , , ]. These observations have been reinforced by more recent large-scale and phase III clinical trials. Baudouin et al. (2025) conducted a phase III multicentre trial comparing preservative-free latanoprost emulsion with a preserved formulation, demonstrating non-inferiority in IOP control while achieving significantly better tolerability and fewer ocular surface adverse events [ ]. Similarly, Czumbel et al. (2024) confirmed the therapeutic equivalence and enhanced comfort of preservative-free generic latanoprost compared with the preserved reference drug (Xalatan ® , Pfizer, Puurs, Belgium) [ ]. Brinkman et al. (2024) reported improved tolerability profiles with preservative-free tafluprost compared to preserved latanoprost, while maintaining comparable IOP-lowering efficacy [ ]. Consistent findings were observed in the COMfort Eye Trial (COMET) by Kandarakis et al. (2024), which confirmed the non-inferiority of preservative-free latanoprost versus Xalatan ® in patients with POAG or OHT, alongside a significant reduction in ocular surface discomfort [ ]. Collectively, these studies confirm that removing preservatives enhances ocular surface safety without compromising antiglaucoma efficacy. The safety of preservative-free ophthalmic formulations has been widely discussed in the literature, as preservatives such as benzalkonium chloride (BAK) are known to induce or exacerbate ocular surface alterations, including epithelial toxicity, tear film instability, and ocular surface inflammation. Several studies have reported improved ocular surface tolerance with preservative-free formulations in comparison with their preserved counterparts [ , , ]. Regarding prostaglandin analogues, earlier investigations primarily focused on BAK-free travoprost formulations, in which alternative preservatives (e.g., polyquaternium-1, SofZia ® ) were used. These studies consistently demonstrated a more favorable ocular surface profile than BAK-preserved travoprost, but they did not evaluate a formulation completely free of preservatives [ , , ]. To our knowledge, the present study is the first to specifically assess the impact of a preservative-free travoprost formulation on the ocular surface. This distinction is important, as even alternative preservatives may exert subclinical or long-term effects on the ocular surface. By eliminating preservatives altogether, preservative-free travoprost offers a potentially safer therapeutic option for patients at risk of ocular surface disease, such as those with concomitant dry eye or requiring long-term intraocular pressure–lowering therapy. Our findings add to the existing body of evidence by demonstrating that preservative-free travoprost maintains efficacy in intraocular pressure control while minimizing ocular surface compromise. This is particularly relevant for glaucoma patients who often require chronic therapy, in whom ocular surface health is a critical determinant of treatment adherence and quality of life. Despite these promising findings, the present study has certain limitations. The absence of objective biomarkers for ocular surface inflammation and the reliance on clinical grading scales may have restricted the sensitivity of surface assessments. A limitation of the present study is the absence of blinding, as it was conducted in an open-label design. Although standardized assessments by a single examiner reduced variability, some degree of observer bias cannot be excluded. An additional consideration is that our study population included both treatment-naïve patients and those who had previously experienced poor tolerability with preserved antiglaucoma therapies. While combining these subgroups follows the methodology of prior studies [ , , ], it may have masked potential differences in response or tolerability between them. We acknowledge this as a limitation and emphasize that larger studies with sufficient statistical power are needed to perform separate analyses of these clinically relevant subgroups. An additional consideration is that our study population included both treatment-naïve patients and those who had previously experienced poor tolerability with preserved antiglaucoma therapies. While combining these subgroups follows the methodology of prior studies [ , , ], it may have masked potential differences in response or tolerability between them. We acknowledge this as a limitation and emphasize that larger studies with sufficient statistical power are needed to perform separate analyses of these clinically relevant subgroups. Future studies incorporating randomized control groups, longer follow-up periods, and objective surface evaluation methods with patient-report outcome using quality of life questionnaires are warranted to validate and expand upon these findings, assess the sustained impact on ocular surface health, and determine whether the observed short-term benefits translate into long-term disease stability and improved patient outcomes. Missing data were handled using a complete-case approach, as the proportion of dropouts was low. It is acknowledged that sensitivity analyses, such as intention-to-treat-based methods, could further assess the robustness of our findings and should be incorporated in future larger, randomized studies to minimize bias related to loss-to-follow-up. The findings of this study have meaningful implications for clinical practice, especially in patients with preexisting OSD. Given that these patients are more susceptible to preservative-induced epithelial toxicity and inflammation, the use of preservative-free travoprost offers a safer and more tolerable therapeutic alternative. Improved ocular surface comfort and reduced hyperemia can enhance treatment adherence and overall quality of life—key factors in successful long-term glaucoma management. Therefore, preservative-free prostaglandin formulations should be strongly considered as first-line therapy, including other preservative-free formulation with the same efficacy, for patients with OSD or those requiring chronic topical treatment. 5. Conclusions In conclusion, preservative-free travoprost offers an effective and well-tolerated treatment for patients with primary open-angle glaucoma, reducing IOP while minimizing the risk of ocular surface disease. The absence of preservatives like BAK in travoprost appears to alleviate many of the adverse effects associated with long-term glaucoma treatment.

documents.title: AAO PPP primary angle closure disease

chunks.content: Introduction Primary angle-closure glaucoma (PACG) occurs in predisposed eyes with a shallow anterior chamber and a narrow anterior chamber angle. It occurs when there is ≥ 180° of iridotrabecular contact with peripheral anterior synechia (PAS), elevated intraocular pressure (IOP), and glaucomatous optic neuropathy [ ]. The aging lens progressively increases in size and thickness and gradually results in a pupillary block. This may cause compression of the peripheral iris, leading to anterior chamber angle stenosis or even closure in predisposed eyes [ , ]. Persistent PAS may block aqueous outflow, leading to Schlemm’s canal endothelial damage and occlusion, and trabecular cell damage [ ]. At the beginning of the disease, the management aims to open the angle and relieve the iris bombé by laser peripheral iridotomy. If the IOP is not controlled, topical antiglaucoma medications may be needed. Surgery should be considered if the topical antiglaucoma medications have failed to control the IOP. Medical treatment is often ineffective in controlling the IOP if there is extensive permanent PAS (≥ 270° of the anterior chamber angle circumference), and a filtering surgery or other type of surgery to control the IOP becomes necessary [ , – ]. Goniosynechialysis, trabeculectomy, lens extraction, or phacotrabeculectomy may be considered surgical solutions [ , , – ]. However, trabeculectomy, either alone or combined with other surgical procedures, is associated with serious complications, e.g., hypotony, shallow anterior chamber, suprachoroidal hemorrhage, malignant glaucoma, and endophthalmitis [ ]. A far more satisfactory approach to the treatment of the early PAS and before the damage of the outflow channels would be lysis of the synechiae, thus re-opening the natural channels of the trabecular meshwork [ , ]. This work aimed to assess the efficacy and safety of combined phacogoniosynechialysis (Phaco-GSL) with viscocanalostomy and Ologen implant for the management of medically uncontrolled PACG with PAS ≥ 270°. Subjects and methods This was a retrospective cohort study. The records of patients with PACG who underwent surgery for PACG for medically uncontrolled IOP, with or without cataracts extraction, between January 2021 and January 2023 were reviewed. PACG was diagnosed based on increased IOP above 21 mmHg and with typical glaucomatous field loss with optic nerve changes compatible with glaucoma. The severity of glaucoma was graded according to Hodapp et al. [ ]. Patients were included if they were ≥ 50 years of age, had mild or moderate PACG with no other ophthalmological disease, apart from cataract, had IOP above 21 mmHg with maximum topical antiglaucoma medications, or if the patient was intolerant to medications and had at least 270° of PAS. Patients with advanced glaucoma and patients with other types of glaucoma were excluded. Also, one-eyed patients were excluded. All patients had a patent laser peripheral iridotomy. The target IOP was defined according to the European Glaucoma Society Guidelines as “The estimate of the mean IOP obtained with treatment that is expected to prevent further glaucomatous damage” [ ]. We set the target IOP according to previous studies: 15 mmHg for moderate glaucoma, and 18 mmHg for mild glaucoma [ , ]. The study protocol was approved by the Institutional Review Board of Suez University, Egypt (SUEZ MED–IRB, Approval No: 44, Date: 08/10/2024). The study adhered to the guidelines of the Declaration of Helsinki. All surgeries were done by one author (AMM). Surgical procedures All surgeries were performed at the Ophthalmology Department of Suez General Hospital (Suez, Egypt). All cases were performed under peribulbar or general anesthesia. Phacoemulsification was done first as follows: a temporal slightly long clear corneal incision 2.8 mm was constructed, and to address the shallow anterior chamber characteristic of angle-closure, a cohesive high-viscosity sodium hyaluronate (Healon GV; Abbott Medical Optics Inc., Santa Ana, CA, USA) was injected to deepen the anterior chamber and protect the corneal endothelium. Then, two paracentesis incisions were created with a 20-gauge MVR blade, with the superior one made about 120° apart from the main incision to leave a space for the viscocanalostomy surgery, and the inferior one is about 90 degrees apart from the main incision. After a continuous curvilinear capsulorhexis was created using capsulorhexis forceps, hydrodissection was performed minimally to avoid further shallowing of the anterior chamber. Nuclear emulsification was executed using a horizontal chopping technique, characterized by lowered aspiration flow rates and vacuum settings to maintain intraoperative stability of the iris-lens diaphragm. Following cortical aspiration, a foldable posterior chamber single-piece hydrophobic acrylic intraocular lens was implanted inside the capsular bag. After that, the anterior chamber was filled with cohesive viscoelastic (Healon). The patient’s head was tilted away from the surgeon, while the operating microscope was angled 45 degrees toward the surgeon. Goniosynechialysis was performed under direct visualization with Swan-Jacob surgical gonioprism (Ocular, Bellevue, WA, USA) using the side of a Sinsky hook (Fig. ). Following cortical aspiration, a foldable posterior chamber single-piece hydrophobic acrylic intraocular lens was implanted inside the capsular bag. After that, the anterior chamber was filled with cohesive viscoelastic (Healon). The patient’s head was tilted away from the surgeon, while the operating microscope was angled 45 degrees toward the surgeon. Goniosynechialysis was performed under direct visualization with Swan-Jacob surgical gonioprism (Ocular, Bellevue, WA, USA) using the side of a Sinsky hook (Fig. ). PAS was carefully released as much as possible, as it is circumferentially accessible. Once completed, the microscope was returned to its upright position, the viscoelastic was removed using bimanual irrigation/aspiration, and stromal hydration was done to close the wounds. Subsequently, viscocanalostomy with Ologen implant was performed according to the described technique [ ]. A corneal traction suture was placed at the superior position with 8 − 0 polyglactin 910 (Vicryl, Ethicon Inc., Bridgewater, NJ, USA). A fornix-based conjunctival flap was created without cautery; hemostasis relied solely on a microsponge saturated with 1/100,000 adrenaline. A 5 × 5 mm superficial scleral flap was fashioned and dissected 2 mm into the clear cornea. A smaller 4 × 4 mm deeper flap was then sculpted until Schlemm’s canal was deroofed. Blunt microsponge dissection to form a descemetic window extending 1–2 mm into the clear cornea over Descemet’s membrane. Vannas’s scissors freed the deep flap edges from the surrounding sclera and excised the flap. The juxtacanalicular trabeculum was excised, after which both Schlemm’s canal ostia were cannulated bilaterally with a viscocanalostomy cannula (EagleVision, Rancho Cucamonga, CA, USA). High-viscosity sodium hyaluronate (Healon GV; Abbott Medical Optics Inc., Santa Ana, CA, USA) was injected into the canal on each side. In cases where synechiae were observed through a trabeculodescmatic window between the trabecular meshwork, Descemet’s membrane, and the iris root, viscoelastic was injected through a paracentesis using a 27-gauge cannula to dissect the iris root from the Descemet’s window and trabecular meshwork. This step was conducted under direct visualization through Descemet’s window to ensure precise separation (Fig. ). Subsequently, a 4 × 4 mm Ologen implant (Model: 862051, 12 mm diameter × 1 mm height; Aeon Astron Europe B.V., Leiden, The Netherlands) was trimmed to match the deep scleral flap dimensions and placed into the subscleral reservoir. The superficial flap was tightly closed over it with four interrupted 10 − 0 nylon sutures (Ethilon, Ethicon Inc., Bridgewater, NJ, USA). Air was injected into the anterior chamber via paracentesis, and the conjunctiva was closed with 8 − 0 polyglactin 910 sutures (Vicryl, Ethicon Inc., Bridgewater, NJ, USA). At any time after surgery, if there was an increase in the IOP, ND: YAG laser goniopuncture was performed using the Ellex Tango Reflex SLT/YAG Multi-Modality Laser (Ellex Medical Lasers Ltd., Australia) in conjunction with a Goldmann three-mirror universal lens (Ocular Instruments, USA) for visualization. The procedure targeted the trabeculo-Descemet’s window to facilitate aqueous outflow. Energy levels were titrated between 3 and 6 mJ, and the number of shots was enough to achieve successful perforation of the Descemet’s membrane, which ranged from 2 to 15 shots. Figures and show the ultrasound biomicroscopy photographs of the subscleral lake one month and one year after surgery. Outcome measures The patients were followed up for one year. The main outcome measures were the IOP control and the number of antiglaucoma medications at the one-year visit. The secondary outcome measure was surgical complications. Criteria for success The success of the surgery was defined at the one-year visit. Complete success was defined as achieving the target IOP without or with one topical antiglaucoma medication, qualified success was defined as achieving the target IOP with two antiglaucoma medications, and failure was defined if the one-year postoperative target IOP could not be attained despite the use of two antiglaucoma medications. Statistical analysis The data were analysed using the Statistical Package for Social Sciences (SPSS) version 28.0 (SPSS Inc., Chicago, Illinois, USA). Continuous variables were presented as mean ± SD. A two-tailed Student t-test was used to determine significance before and after the intervention within the same group. Nonparametric data are displayed by median and range. For comparing data on paired analysis, the Wilcoxon signed-rank test was used for comparing indecently. Categorical variables were expressed as numbers and percentages. A p-value < 0.05 was deemed statistically significant. In cases where patients were classified as failures during the follow-up period, the baseline IOP and the last-measured IOP before directing them to another line of treatment were utilized for follow-up statistical analysis. Results Twenty-seven patients were eligible to be included in the study. The demographic data for patients are summarized in Table . There were 7 patients with clear lenses and 20 patients with cataracts. There were 13 eyes with mild glaucoma and 14 eyes with moderate glaucoma. Nine eyes were controlled for IOP without goniopuncture (33.3%), but a goniopuncture was needed in 18 eyes (66.7%) to control the IOP. One year after surgery, there was a significant reduction in IOP and in the number of glaucoma medications from the preoperative levels ( p < 0.001 in both parameters), Table . The mean decrease in IOP was 13.33 ± 4.07 mmHg (range: 8–21 mmHg), and the mean percentage of reduction in IOP was 48.11 ± 9.85% (range: 26.7–63.6). Figure shows the mean IOP ± SD levels from baseline to the one-year follow-up after Surgery. The mean reduction of glaucoma medications was 2.74 ± 1.10 (median = 3, range: 0–4), and the mean percentage of reduction of glaucoma medication was 76.23 ± 1.1% (median = 100%, range: 0-100%). At the one-year postoperatively, two eyes (7.4%) were classified as failure, six eyes (22.2) as qualified success, and 19 eyes (70.4%) were classified as complete success; Fig. . There was a significant increase in the mean postoperative VA than the preoperative level ( p < 0.001), Table . All patients with clear lenses retained the same preoperative visual acuity except for one patient whose postoperative visual acuity decreased from 6/7.5 to 6/10 (Snellen’s acuity). For those patients, the mean preoperatively VA was 0.06 ± 0.06 (log MAR), and the mean postoperative VA was 0.08 ± 0.08 (log MAR) with no statistically significant difference ( p = 0.36). The visual acuity for patients with cataracts improved postoperatively to near normal visual acuity with a mean ± SD = 0.88 ± 1.7. The lowest postoperative best-corrected visual acuity for all patients was 6/12, which occurred in 2 eyes. Malignant glaucoma occurred in three patients (11.1%) on the first-week-visit. All cases were treated effectively, and the IOP was controlled at the one-month visit. Malignant glaucoma was diagnosed by an acute rise in IOP and a shallow anterior chamber in the presence of a patent peripheral iridotomy. One case was completely resolved after YAG-Laser posterior capsulotomy using the same Laser machine in conjunction with atropine sulphate 1% eye drops three times daily, and the other two cases were treated by pars plana vitrectomy with surgical posterior capsulotomy. Pupillary membrane occurred in 2 eyes (7.4%). The membrane resolved completely by increasing the frequency of the postoperative steroid eye drops. Minimal hyphema occurred in one eye (3.7%), which resolved without treatment. Discussion The formation of PAS in PACG may be a slow, gradual process, and the IOP may increase slowly and unnoticed by the patient, and most patients are asymptomatic till the advanced stage [ , ]. Lens extraction to relieve pupillary block and widen the anterior chamber angle, combined with goniosynechialysis to eliminate PAS and the possible return of the normal aqueous outflow channels, is a realistic way to control IOP. All patients in this study had PACG with at least 270° of PAS with patent iridotomy, high IOP, and 3–4 antiglaucoma medications. Our patients did not experience an acute attack, and the period of the syenechial closure could not be determined; hence, we were unable to estimate the extent of damage to the outflow channels. Together with the presence of ≥ 270° of PAS, a surgical intervention is mandatory. Also, Sihota et al. have found that the area of trabecular damage is more extensive than the visible PAS on gonioscopy [ ]. An eye with a very narrow angle or a thick lens may continue to have angle closure and rise of IOP despite a patent iridectomy [ ]. The damage of the outflow channels may result in a failure of control of IOP after Phaco-GSL alone [ ]. We chose to combine Phaco-GSL and viscocanalostomy to ensure patent and continuous aqueous outflow through the subscleral lake, as proved by ultrasonic biomicroscopy, aiming to achieve long-term control of the IOP, open the outflow channel, minimize the failure rate and the need for antiglaucoma medications, and avoid the complications of other surgical procedures, e.g., trabeculectomy. The overall success of our study was 92.6%, which is comparable to the results of Tham et al., who achieved IOP control in 91.7% after using combined phacotrabeculectomy with adjunctive mitomycin

may result in a failure of control of IOP after Phaco-GSL alone [ ]. We chose to combine Phaco-GSL and viscocanalostomy to ensure patent and continuous aqueous outflow through the subscleral lake, as proved by ultrasonic biomicroscopy, aiming to achieve long-term control of the IOP, open the outflow channel, minimize the failure rate and the need for antiglaucoma medications, and avoid the complications of other surgical procedures, e.g., trabeculectomy. The overall success of our study was 92.6%, which is comparable to the results of Tham et al., who achieved IOP control in 91.7% after using combined phacotrabeculectomy with adjunctive mitomycin C [ ]. Two-thirds of our patients experienced an increase in intraocular pressure after it was controlled. In these patients, intraocular pressure was controlled after goniopuncture. This highlights the importance of making this intervention an available option. The IOP target for defining success in our study has been set to be 18 mmHg for mild glaucoma and 15 mmHg for moderate glaucoma, which is less than that of Tham et al., who used 21 mmHg as a target level. The lower the IOP before reaching hypotony, the better the control of glaucoma. Tanihara et al. have found that the success rate of GSL in aphakic eyes is twice that in phakic ones in eyes with 180° to 270° of PAS. This indicates that lens removal with GSL results in better IOP control in eyes with PACG [ ]. In the EAGLE study, Azuara-Blanco et al., in a randomized study, found that early clear-lens extraction is superior to laser peripheral iridotomy plus topical medications in the treatment of PACG in patients with PAS of ≤ 180° (20–180°) on indentation gonioscopy. They recommended clear-lens extraction to be the first line of treatment in such conditions [ ]. Yu et al. recommended Phaco-GSL should be the first-line of treatment in patients with PAS > 180°, as the prolonged PAS and chamber angle closure may lead to irreversible damage of the trabecular meshwork and may result in failure of IOP control after Phaco-GSL surgery [ ]. Combined phacoemulsification and viscogoniosynechialysis has been found to be an effective and safe treatment to control the IOP in patients with refractory acute angle-closure glaucoma by Razeghinejad [ ]. Zhuo et al. have found that phacoemulsification is more effective in patients with acute PACG than in patients with chronic PACG in patients with synechial angle closure of 180° or more. Their patients had ≥ 90° of angle open with no PAS, and the maximum length of the acute attack of ACG was 2 months (before permanent outflow channel destruction) [ ]. Phacoviscocanalostomy has been found to be comparable to phacotrabeculectomy in controlling the IOP in primary open-angle glaucoma with fewer complications [ ]. In this study, there was a significant reduction in preoperative medications, with more than half of the eyes (14 eyes; 52%) controlled without any antiglaucoma drugs, and 5 eyes (20%) controlled with one antiglaucoma topical medication. We experienced a high rate of postoperative malignant glaucoma (which was successfully treated). This may be due to the short axial length, extensive anterior chamber synechiae, and/or the combined procedure. Except for malignant glaucoma, the complications in this study were few and minor, with no major consequences. Two eyes did not achieve the target IOP and were considered failures; one eye had an IOP of 19 mmHg with three antiglaucoma drugs, and one eye had an IOP above 21 mmHg (22 mmHg with four antiglaucoma medications). In this study, the visual results were good. All patients with clear lenses retained the same preoperative visual acuity, except for one patient with clinically insignificant loss of postoperative visual acuity. All patients with cataracts improved postoperatively to near-normal visual acuity. Our findings indicate that combined Phaco-GSL with viscocanalostomy is an effective procedure with minimal complications for controlling IOP, achieving the targeted IOP, and reducing reliance on antiglaucoma medications in PACG. The procedure demonstrated an overall success rate of 93%, with a mean IOP reduction of 13.33 mmHg and an average decrease of 3.0 antiglaucoma medications. This study addressed the management of PACG when the PAS is ≥ 270°, a topic that has been infrequently explored in previous research. To the best of our knowledge, it is the first to incorporate Phaco-GSL with viscocanalostomy and an Ologen implant for these specific cases. However, the study’s limitations include its retrospective design, small sample size, and short follow-up period. To confirm the long-term efficacy of this combined approach in PACG with PAS of 270° or more, larger-scale randomized trials with larger sample sizes and longer follow-up periods are needed.

Thrombosis (occlusion) of the central retinal vein (RCVO) and its branches is one of the main causes of loss or sig- nificant decrease in vision, including in people of working age, while RCVO is the second most common retinal vascular disease after diabetic retinopathy. The incidence rates steadily increase with age, amounting to 0.7% in the 49–60 age group and reach- ing 4.6% in people over 80 years old. Acute violation of retinal venous blood flow often leads to retinal ischemia, triggering the mechanism of activation of endothelial vascular growth factor (VEGF). In a quarter of patients, occlusions of the retinal veins and its branches initially proceed according to the ischemic type, which is characterized by the formation of extensive non-per- fused retinal zones occupying an area of 10 or more areas of the optic nerve head (optic nerve disc) according to fluorescent angiography (FAG). In 34% of such patients, the non-ischemic type of venous occlusion becomes ischemic within 3 years. 374 МЕДИЦИНСКИЙ СОВЕТ 2021;(12):374–378 © Гамидов А.А., Сурнина З.В., Андреева И.В., 2021 Aim. To develop an optimal algorithm for the management of patients with operated neovascular uncompensated glauco- ma against the background of occlusion of the central retinal vein. Materials and methods. Two patients with operated secondary neovascular glaucoma of stage III-c. In the combined sequential therapy, the anti-­VEGF medication Aflibercept (0.5 mg) was used, laser coagulation of residual newly formed vessels, laser recon- struction in the surgical area, contact transcleral cyclolazercoagulation, and laser coagulation of the peripheral parts of the reti- na were performed. Results. The combined sequential treatment, combined with the appointment of antihypertensive drugs in drops, allowed to stabilize the level of IOP. IOP indicators remained at the level of normal values during 1 year of follow-up. Conclusion. The use of combined laser technologies and anti-­VEGF therapy allows potentiating and prolonging the hypotensive effect in the treatment of patients with operated secondary refractory neovascular glaucoma against the background of occlusion of the central retinal vein. chunks.content: 1. Introduction Systemic autoimmune diseases are characterized by a variety of organ involvement and immunological features, which are the basis for different classification criteria [ – ]. However, presentation, disease course, response to treatment and progression to end-organ damage of individual systemic autoimmune diseases is heterogeneous [ , ]. In addition, systemic autoimmune diseases share clinical and laboratory manifestations or overlap, increasing diagnosis and treatment challenges in clinical care [ , ]. Immunologically, systemic autoimmune diseases are characterized by activation of the innate and adaptive immune system, leading to loss of self-tolerance, autoantibody formation and tissue destruction [ , , ]. Genetic studies have shown that systemic autoimmune diseases are complex diseases that share susceptibility genes, commonly including genes in the major histocompatibility locus [ , – ]. However, genetic similarities account for less than 30 % of the phenotypic variance observed [ , ]. Epigenetic mechanisms (DNA methylation, histone modifications, microRNA, RNA helicases) in genetically predisposed individuals have an important role in disease-onset, phenotypic variation and response to treatment [ – ]. More recently, whole blood transcriptome and methylome analysis of 7 different systemic autoimmune diseases [rheumatoid arthritis (RA), systemic sclerosis (SSc), primary Sjögren’s syndrome/disease (pSD), systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), primary antiphospholipid syndrome (pAPS), mixed connective tissue disease (MCTD) and undifferentiated connective tissue disease (UCTD)] has identified and validated 3 pathogenic clusters [ ]. The clusters represent a unique inflammatory, lymphoid, and interferon driven pattern during diseases activity [ ]. A fourth pattern was identified where predominantly healthy controls, low-disease activity and remission patients were represented [ ]. In a longitudinal cohort, patients maintained the same pathogenic cluster during flares and remission [ ]. In systemic autoimmune conditions, the involvement of the central nervous system (CNS) and peripheral nervous system (PNS) is frequently observed and associated with high morbidity and mortality [ – ]. The wide range of neuropsychiatric (NP) manifestations associated with systemic autoimmune diseases, as well as the complex pathogenesis, the presence of concomitant comorbidities, the lack of uniformity in the definitions of NP events, and the absence of protocols for establishing a causal relationship between symptoms and autoimmune disease can hinder timely diagnosis and delay the introduction of specific therapies [ ]. In this context, the objective of this study is to provide a narrative review of the main NP manifestations related to systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and primary Sjogren’s Disease (pSD) disease through the description of pathogenic mechanisms, clinical presentation, immunological features and imaging. 2. Methodology This narrative review was conducted through national and international articles available in the Scientific Electronic Library Online (SciELO) and PubMed databases, related to the description of neurological and psychiatric manifestations in patients with rheumatologic diseases of interest in this study (Systemic Lupus Erythematosus, Sjögren’s Syndrome, Disease). The search was conducted using the following descriptors in Portuguese and English: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus; Sjogren’s Syndrome, each correlated with the Boolean operator “AND” followed by the terms: Neuropsychiatric manifestations, Neurological manifestations, Psychiatric manifestations, or terms alluding to these conditions. The period established for article selection was between 1990 and December 2024, and inclusion criteria were related to full texts available in Portuguese, English, or French. 3. Classification criteria for neuropsychiatric manifestations In the consensus developed by the American College of Rheumatology (ACR), nineteen clinical syndromes related to NPSLE were defined, divided topographically into manifestations affecting the CNS (aseptic meningitis, cerebrovascular disease, demyelinating syndrome, headache, movement disorders, myelopathy, seizure, acute confusional state, anxiety disorders, cognitive dysfunction, mood disorders, and psychosis) and the PNS (acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy, autonomic disorders, isolated mononeuropathy or multiple mononeuropathy, myasthenia gravis, cranial neuropathy, plexopathy, and polyneuropathy confirmed by electroneuromyography) [ ]. There are no specific tests or prognostic markers for the recognition of most NP diseases associated with SLE. Therefore, the diagnosis of such conditions is based on clinical, laboratory, and radiological findings, following extensive investigation and exclusion of more probable alternative diagnoses [ ]. In a cross-sectional study, the prevalence of neuropsychiatric manifestations according to the ACR nomenclature was 46 % [ ]. However, when mild neuropsychiatric syndromes (mild cognitive deficit, headache, mild depression, anxiety and electroneuromyography-negative polyneuropathy) were excluded, the overall prevalence increased to 91 % [ ]. Based on distinct pathophysiology, CNS manifestations can further be subdivided into focal and diffuse [ , ] ( ). Although the pathophysiology of these manifestations is different, the manifestations often overlap in SLE patients. In pSD there are no validated diagnostic or classification criteria. Several authors have proposed to classify the neuropsychiatric manifestations according to anatomy (central, peripheral and autonomic) [ , ]. CNS manifestations are additionally classified in diffuse, focal and spinal cord involvement ( ) [ , ]. Many NP manifestations are diagnosed based on specific society criteria [ , ]. More recently a joint collaboration between the American College of Rheumatology, American Academy of Neurology

be subdivided into focal and diffuse [ , ] ( ). Although the pathophysiology of these manifestations is different, the manifestations often overlap in SLE patients. In pSD there are no validated diagnostic or classification criteria. Several authors have proposed to classify the neuropsychiatric manifestations according to anatomy (central, peripheral and autonomic) [ , ]. CNS manifestations are additionally classified in diffuse, focal and spinal cord involvement ( ) [ , ]. Many NP manifestations are diagnosed based on specific society criteria [ , ]. More recently a joint collaboration between the American College of Rheumatology, American Academy of Neurology and Sjögren’s Syndrome Foundation has developed evidence-based guidelines for the evaluation and management of peripheral nervous system manifestations, however they have not been published as a full paper yet [ ]. 4. Epidemiology The prevalence of NP manifestations of SLE in the CNS can vary from 21 to 96 %. This wide range can be explained by both the variability of clinical manifestations and the lack of specific diagnostic criteria for such conditions, as well as the heterogeneity of the studied populations [ – ]. Involvement of the PNS by SLE is apparently less frequent, but also less studied [ ]. A retrospective cohort study with 1224 patients demonstrated PNS involvement in 6.9 % of patients, of which 68 % of cases were directly attributed to SLE [ ]. NP symptoms related to SLE generally occur in the first two years of disease, in association with systemic disease activity [ , ]. Exceptions are stroke and cognitive dysfunction, which generally occur at later stages of the disease and often associated with corticosteroid use or cardiovascular disease [ , , ]. SLE patients can present one single NP event, however around 17–60 % present at least a second event during their disease course [ ]. The spectrum of severity is broad and includes both nonspecific symptoms and potentially life-threatening situations. Any region of the CNS or PNS can be affected, either primarily (resulting from immune-mediated mechanisms involving pathogenic autoantibodies, cytokines, or cells) or secondarily (due to infections related to immunosuppression, adverse effects of medications in use, and concomitant metabolic or autoimmune disorders) [ , ]. Important to notice is that 60 % of NP manifestations are due to secondary causes, and careful evaluation is necessary for adequate treatment ( )[ , ]. pSD is characterized by sicca syndrome, however a wide spectrum of clinical manifestations has been described varying from mild disease limited to exocrine glands to severe multi-systemic involvement, including, but not limited to lungs, skin, kidney and the nervous system [ , – ]. Neurological manifestations can involve both CNS and the PNS, although CNS involvement is less common [ , , – ]. Neurological manifestations occur in 8.5 % to 70 % of patients with pSD (average of 20 %) and may precede sicca symptoms in 40 % to 93 % of cases in up to 2 years [ , , ]. The discrepancy between studies results mainly from the lack of well-defined diagnostic criteria for recognizing this condition and the fact that cohorts may come from different specialties (e.g rheumatology or neurology) [ ]. It is estimated that the CNS manifestations occur in 2 % to 5 % pSD. The prevalence varies widely, as lower estimates refer only to focal structural changes, while the highest estimate also includes functional changes. Headache (47 %), cognitive dysfunction (44 %), and mood disorders (38 %) are the manifestations more frequently reported [ ]. 5. Pathophysiology The pathophysiology of NPSLE is multifactorial and involve autoantibody production, microangiopathy complement activation and intrathecal production of proinflammatory cytokines ( ) [ , ]. These mechanisms lead to a predominant inflammatory phenotype, responsible for diffuse NP manifestations or a predominant vascular phenotype that characterizes focal manifestations [ , ]. Atherosclerosis has to be ruled out, since SLE patients have a higher risk of premature atherosclerosis [ , ]. Histopathology studies demonstrate that microvasculopathy is the most common findings, characterized by multifocal microinfarcts, cortical atrophy, gross infarcts, hemorrhage, ischemic demyelination, and patchy multiple-sclerosis-like demyelination [ , ]. In SLE, systemic inflammation and autoantibody production can lead to blood–brain barrier (BBB) disruption, allowing cytokines and autoantibodies to enter the brain and activate local glial cells or neuronal death [ ]. Pro-inflammatory cytokines/analytes or autoantibodies that up-regulate the expression of adhesion proteins on endothelial cells, facilitate BBB rupture [ ]. Soluble serum levels of inter-cellular adhesion molecule 1 (ICAM-1) increase when SLE patient is in disease activity and normalize with remission strengthening the hypothesis that activated endothelial cells and a lack of integrity of the BBB might be an essential requisite for disease activity in the brain [ – ]. However other mechanism involving the neuroimmune interface have been identify, such as breach in the meningeal barrier, transport

enter the brain and activate local glial cells or neuronal death [ ]. Pro-inflammatory cytokines/analytes or autoantibodies that up-regulate the expression of adhesion proteins on endothelial cells, facilitate BBB rupture [ ]. Soluble serum levels of inter-cellular adhesion molecule 1 (ICAM-1) increase when SLE patient is in disease activity and normalize with remission strengthening the hypothesis that activated endothelial cells and a lack of integrity of the BBB might be an essential requisite for disease activity in the brain [ – ]. However other mechanism involving the neuroimmune interface have been identify, such as breach in the meningeal barrier, transport of immune effector cells through the glymphatic circulatory system or infiltration of leucocytes and antibodies through choroid plexus [ , ]. Several studies have analyzed the role of inflammatory processes in the manifestations of CNS. Interleukins (IL), tumor necrosis factors (TNF) and metalloproteinase have been shown to be increased in serum and CSF in patients with CNS manifestations and even associated with some specific clinical manifestations and MRI findings [ , ]. Inflammatory mediator in serum and plasma are associated with NP SLE in different cohorts [ ]. IL-6 level in the CSF or serum of NP SLE has been associated with NP SLE, especially acute confusional state, headache and cognitive impairment [ – ]. A multicenter retrospective studied showed that the sensitivity and specificity of CSF IL-6 for diagnosis of lupus psychosis was 87.5 % and 92.3 %, respectively, indicating that CSF IL-6 might be an effective marker for the diagnosis of lupus psychosis [ ]. Serum and CSF levels IL-4, IL-6, IL-10 TNF-α, BAFF, APRIL, INF-α and IFN-γ have been studied in NP SLE, with conflicting results [ – ]. Increased levels of TNF- α has been associated with depressive symptoms in SLE [ ]. Increased CSF INF-α has been shown to be increased in NP SLE and to cause microglia-associated synaptic loss [ , – ]. In lupus prone mice an association between peripheral IFNα and microglia activation was observed [ ]. CSF and serum IFN-γ levels have been shown to be associated with diffuse brain atrophy and axonal damage [ , ]. CX3CL1, CSF MCP-1/CCL2, RANTES/CCL5 and IL-8/CXCL8 levels are elevated in the cerebrospinal fluid of patients with active NPSLE [ , ]. Interferon-gamma inducible protein-10 (IP-10)/CXCL10 has been observed upregulated in NP SLE [ , – ]. Serum matrix metalloproteinase 9 (MP-9 M), serum S100B and S100A8/A9 protein levels have also been shown to be increased in NPSLE patients. The presence of these proteins reflects continuing neurological damage and are useful for identifying patients with cognitive impairment [ , , ]. A key feature in SLE and NP manifestations is the autoantibody production. Approximately 116 autoantibodies have been associated with SLE, of which 20 (11 specific to the brain and 9 systemic) have been controversially related to NP syndromes attributed to SLE ( ) [ ]. Most of the studied antibodies lack clinical applicability, either due to being tests that are not widely available or not being widely accepted as diagnostic criteria. Antiphospholipid antibodies (aPL) are present in more than 45 % of patients diagnosed with SLE, this group includes lupus anticoagulant, anti-cardiolipin antibodies, and anti-Beta 2 glycoprotein 1 (anti-B2GP1) antibodies [ ]. There is evidence that aPL (especially lupus anticoagulant) is related to cerebrovascular diseases, especially thrombosis and stroke. They may also be implicated in the occurrence of seizures, movement disorders, cognitive impairment and myelopathy [ , , ]. Anti-ribosomal P antibodies (anti-P) are positive in 6 to 46 % of patients, are significantly associated with lupus psychosis and depression [ – ]. There are animal models and in vitro studies that supports the involvement of anti-P in the pathogenesis of NP manifestations [ ]. In vitro, anti-P antibodies bind peripheral blood monocytes and induce TNF production [ ]. Increased serum TNFα production promotes local CNS inflammation, resulting in BBB disruption and entrance of cytokines and autoantibodies into the CNS [ , , ]. Once in the CNS, anti-P bind to the limbic and olfactory system, brain regions implicated in memory, mood and smell, and which have been reported to be affected in SLE [ , , , ]. Anti- N -methyl- d -aspartate receptor antibodies (anti-NMDAR) and NR 2 antibodies expressed in 30–40 % of patients are related to the pathogenesis of cognitive impairment and acute confusional state [ , ]. The NR2A messenger RNA (mRNA) has higher concentrations in the cerebral cortex, hippocampus, and cerebellum and is widely distributed in the brain, while the NR2B transcript is selectively present in the forebrain, with higher levels of expression located in the cerebral cortex, hippocampus, septum, caudate-putamen, and olfactory bulb [ , ]. Anti-NMDAR antibodies mediate apoptotic cell death of neurons in vitro and in vivo [ ]. NR2 and anti-NMDAR antibodies in serum

receptor antibodies (anti-NMDAR) and NR 2 antibodies expressed in 30–40 % of patients are related to the pathogenesis of cognitive impairment and acute confusional state [ , ]. The NR2A messenger RNA (mRNA) has higher concentrations in the cerebral cortex, hippocampus, and cerebellum and is widely distributed in the brain, while the NR2B transcript is selectively present in the forebrain, with higher levels of expression located in the cerebral cortex, hippocampus, septum, caudate-putamen, and olfactory bulb [ , ]. Anti-NMDAR antibodies mediate apoptotic cell death of neurons in vitro and in vivo [ ]. NR2 and anti-NMDAR antibodies in serum and CSF have been associated with NP manifestations, especially cognitive impairment, depression and acute confusional state, in addition to reduced volumes of the limbic structures, such as hippocampus and amygdalae [ – ]. Anti-neuronal antibodies (anti-N) have been identified in both sera and CSF in NP SLE, suggesting that symptoms may arise from an antibody and neuronal cell membrane interactions [ , ]. Cytokines and autoantibodies can further be stimulated through oxidative stress and kalikrein (KYN) pathway, contributing to pathogenesis of NP SLE (ref) [ – ]. Oxidative stress is directly linked to cognitive dysfunction [ ]. Oxidative stress also causes (1) mitochondrial dysfunction and immune dysregulation, and (2) aberrant lipid metabolism leading to enhanced autoantibody production [ – ]. IFNα, induces indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase (IDO) present in immune cells in the periphery and brain and involved in the pathogenesis of SLE [ , ]. KYN /tryptophan (KYN/TRP) pathway is catalysed by the enzyme IDO into KYN that is further metabolised to either quinolinic acid (QA) and kynurenic acid (KA) [ ]. As an NMDAR agonist, QA can cause glutamatergic excitotoxicity, while KA is an NMDAR antagonist that can protect neurons from excitotoxic damage [ , , , ]. Genetic polymorphisms have also been associated with NPSLE. Single-nucleotide polymorphisms of the TREX1 gene can increase the expression of type I interferons (IFN) and, thus, are related to NPSLE, particularly seizures [ , , ]. Stroke, on the other hand, has been related to polymorphisms in the HLA-DRB1 (HLA-DRB1*04/*13 genotype) [ ] and STAT4 [ ] genes. Also, accumulating polymorphisms related to general SLE manifestations also can increase the chance of NPSLE [ ]. Cohort studies have shown that neurological involvement is more frequently observed in pSD with positive SSA/Ro antibodies and the presence of constitutional symptoms, low complement levels and extraglandular involvement [ – ]. The pathogenesis of neurological involvement in pSD appears to be related to a combination of vasculopathy and autoimmunity [ ]. The pathophysiology of CNS involvement in pSD is an immune-mediated small-vessel vasculopathy [ ]. Small-vessel vasculitis occurs in lesser extend [ ]. This hypothesis is based on presence of increased lymphocytes and protein, increased IgG index, oligoclonal bands, intrathecal activated terminal complements in CSF of pSD associated with MRI and angiograph findings, however, the lack of pathological specimen from brain biopsies limits definitive histopathological diagnosis [ ]. Anti-Ro antibodies (SSA) targeting the interferon (IFN)-inducible Ro protein are found in about 70 % of patients [ – ]. Anti SSA/Ro was associated with a more extensive CNS involvement, including transverse myelitis, peripheral neuropathy, encephalitis, and dementia [ , ]. Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD) is an autoimmune astrocytopathy, due to the production of pathogenic antibodies against aquaporin-4 (AQP4) expressed on the foot of astrocytes and often associated with other systemic autoimmune diseases, such as pSD [ ]. NMOSD patients with anti-SSA/Ro antibody had higher EDSS score and the relapsed more frequently [ ]. A Anti D-aminoacyl-tRNA deacylase (DTD2) has been observed in higher frequency in SSA positive pSD patients and has been shown to be associated with neurodegeneration from misfolded proteins in mice [ – ]. Anti-La antibodies (SSB) are reported in 30 to 40 % of patients with pSD, they are more related to psychiatric symptoms such as psychosis, depression and anxiety [ ]. Antibodies against glutamate receptors are observed in 20 % of patients with pSD, they are associated with movement disorders and epilepsy [ – ]. Antibodies against the NR2 subtype of the N -methyl- d -aspartate receptor (anti-NR2): Studies have shown that anti-NR2 antibodies are related to gray matter loss in the hippocampus in patients with pSD, which is associated with cognitive dysfunction and depression [ ]. The mechanisms underlying PNS are multifactorial, and are not completely elucidated [ ]. pSD patients with sensory neuronopathy have evidence of multifocal infiltration of dorsal root ganglia by T CD8 (+) lymphocytes with direct neuronal aggression in pathological reports [ , ]. The presence of capillaries fenestration allows autoreactive cells to reach the target, leading to degeneration of sensory neuron bodies and subsequent degeneration of peripheral and central axonal projections. The frequency of antibodies against the transmembrane protein FGFR3 is observed predominantly in pSD with immune-mediated

in patients with pSD, which is associated with cognitive dysfunction and depression [ ]. The mechanisms underlying PNS are multifactorial, and are not completely elucidated [ ]. pSD patients with sensory neuronopathy have evidence of multifocal infiltration of dorsal root ganglia by T CD8 (+) lymphocytes with direct neuronal aggression in pathological reports [ , ]. The presence of capillaries fenestration allows autoreactive cells to reach the target, leading to degeneration of sensory neuron bodies and subsequent degeneration of peripheral and central axonal projections. The frequency of antibodies against the transmembrane protein FGFR3 is observed predominantly in pSD with immune-mediated sensory neuronopathy, however its role in the pathogenesis of PNS has to be established [ ]. pSD-related multiple mononeuropathy is secondary to vasculitic changes with periarteriolar cellular invasion and indirect axonal damage [ ]. Anti-SSA/Ro and anti SSB/La antibodies are also associated with PNS involvement, especially functional abnormalities [ ]. Patients with positive Anti-SSA/Ro and anti SSB/La antibodies had reduced motor and sensory excitability relative to negative autoantibody group, suggesting that these antibodies are related to nodal and internodal dysfunction in large sensory and motor fibers [ ]. Therefore, the pathophysiology of PNS damage in seronegative and seropositive SS may be different [ ]. 6. Clinical manifestations 6.1. Central nervous system involvement 6.1.1. Cerebrovascular events Cerebrovascular events (CVEs) encompass in order of frequency stroke, transient ischemia (TIA), subarachnoid/intracranial hemorrhage, chronic multifocal ischemia and cerebral venous thrombosis (CVT). CVE occur in approximately 5 % of SLE patients [ , ]. Compared to non-SLE patients, SLE patients have a twofold to threefold higher risk of CVE [ ]. The risk of stroke seems to be higher in black and Hispanic SLE patients [ ]. CVE events attributed to SLE activity SLE (cerebral vasculitis) usually occur early in the course of the disease and are often accompanied by evidence of activity in other organs; those related to APS or other related cardiovascular risk factors can occur at any time, in patients with either active or inactive SLE [ ]. CVE occurrence appears to be more frequent in individuals with positivity for Anti-ß2 GP1-IgG and Anti-ß2 GP1-IgM [ ]. The frequency of CVE increases with disease duration and previous CVE [ – ]. CVE account for approximately 10 to 15 % of deaths in patients with SLE, with ischemic cerebrovascular accidents being the most frequent event [ , ]. In addition, SLE with CVE have poor stroke functional outcome [ ]. Although premature atherosclerosis has been demonstrated in pSD, an increased risk of ischemic stroke is still debated [ – ]. Two nationwide cohort studies demonstrated that pSD and controls had a similar incidence of ischemic stroke, however, pSD patients with stroke have an increased risk for hospitalization (SIR = 2.57), especially in the first two years after the ischemic event [ – ]. Another population-based multicenter study showed that pSD patients had a significant increased risk of cerebrovascular event (2.5 %) when compared to general population (1.4 %) [ ]. A meta-analysis including 14 studies confirmed an increased risk of cerebrovascular events with a relative risk of 1.44 [95 % CI 1.43–1.49], however, without increased risk of mortality [ ]. 6.1.2. Cognitive dysfunction Cognitive dysfunction is a frequent complaint in SLE and has a pooled prevalence of approximately 40 % [ ]. It is characterized by attention deficit, abnormal processing speed, and impairment of executive functions, constituting one of the most frequent NP findings in patients with SLE [ – ]. It tends to present insidiously and fluctuate over time. Dementia is rarely reported in SLE [ – ]. It has a multifactorial etiology, and risk factors described include presence of other NP manifestations, positivity for aPL antibodies, use of glucocorticoids, low level of education, and structural brain abnormalities [ , , , ]. The ACR committee has proposed a standard 1-h battery of neuropsychologic tests [ ]. Evidence on the reliability and validity of this battery was established, however universal use is restricted since not all tests are validates in different languages and the absence of specialized professionals [ ]. Self-assessment does not correlate with objective cognitive evaluation [ ]. Several screening or automated testing investigational methods have been proposed, come with conflicting result, such as the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MOCA) [ ] and cognitive symptom inventory (CSI). More evidence have been published on the construct and criterion validity [ , ] of the Automated Neuropsychological Assessment Metrics (ANAM) compared to the ACR battery [ , , , , ]. MRI is the gold standard imaging evaluation in cognitive impairment. Global and regional atrophy, especially hippocampal and corpus callosum involvement, has been associated with the presence of cognitive impairment [ , ]. Diffusion Tension Imaging (DTI), magnetic resonance spectroscopy, dynamic enhanced and functional MRI has been useful in SLE patients with normal

conflicting result, such as the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MOCA) [ ] and cognitive symptom inventory (CSI). More evidence have been published on the construct and criterion validity [ , ] of the Automated Neuropsychological Assessment Metrics (ANAM) compared to the ACR battery [ , , , , ]. MRI is the gold standard imaging evaluation in cognitive impairment. Global and regional atrophy, especially hippocampal and corpus callosum involvement, has been associated with the presence of cognitive impairment [ , ]. Diffusion Tension Imaging (DTI), magnetic resonance spectroscopy, dynamic enhanced and functional MRI has been useful in SLE patients with normal MRI and cognitive impairment, showing cerebral dysfunction in areas that correspond to cognitive dysfunction [ , , – ]. Cognitive impairment has been described to occur in pSD in up to 80 % of patients and both subjective and objective cognitive dysfunction has been reported [ , – ]. In the majority of patients, cognitive impairment remains stable overtime and progression to dementia is rarely reported [ – ]. The cognitive deficits associated with pSD are related to fronto-subcortical dysfunctions, resulting in impairment of executive functions. Visual-spatial disturbances and deficits in long-term and short-term memory have also been reported [ ]. Cognitive dysfunction has been associated with pain, depression and reduced quality of life and the presence of anti-NR2 antibodies [ , , , , – ]. However, studies have also shown the role of immune-mediated mechanism in cognitive dysfunction in pSD, with evidence of inflammation in CSF and neuroimaging studies [ , – ]. MRI is normal in the vast majority of cases, but hippocampal volume reduction and hypoperfusion in the white matter of frontoparietal subcortical regions has been described [ , , , ]. White matter lesions are observed in 48 % of pSD and associated with CNS manifestations and cardiovascular risk factors [ ]. 6.1.3. Headache Headache is a common finding in patients with SLE with frequencies similar to healthy individuals, and rarely related to disease activity. The pooled prevalence of headache in SLE is 26.8 % [ ]. Lupus related headache, is a rare manifestation, occurring in less than 2 % of SLE patients [ ]. The most common subtype of chronic headache in SLE patients is migraine [ , – ]. SLE patients with headache have impaired quality of life and higher irreversible damage than SLE patients without headache [ , ]. The prevalence of headache is similar in pSD when compared to general population [ ], however, pSD patients have more severe headaches and greater burden [ , ]. In pSD, migraine is the headache type most frequently observed and associated with the presence of SSA-Ro antibodies and Raynaud’s phenomenon [ ]. pSD with headache have functional changes in neuroimaging studies (reduction of N -acetyl aspartate levels in magnetic resonance spectroscopy and haemodynamic dysfunction at ultrasonographic evaluation), but no evidence of vasculitis [ ]. These findings suggest that headache in pSD may be secondary to endothelial dysfunction of the cerebral microcirculation or a potential inflammation-mediated shift of the neurovascular coupling [ ]. 6.1.4. Seizures Seizures attributed to SLE occur in 2 to 8 % [ ] and can be focal or generalized. Risk factors for seizures include treatment with glucocorticoids, positive aPL and anti-Smith (anti-Sm) antibodies, previous psychosis, neuropathy, proteinuria, low C3 levels, and active disease [ , ]. The minority of SLE patients need more than 6 months of antiepileptic treatment [ – ]. Recurrence of seizures is rare and associated with positive aPL antibodies, structural abnormalities on MRI, cumulative damage and interictal abnormalities on EEG [ , ]. Seizures have been reported to occur in 2–8 % of pSD, however, no specific association with disease activity, antibody profile and MRI findings has been described [ , ]. In children with systemic autoimmune disorders, including pSD, a 5-fold increased risk of seizures and epilepsy has been described [ ]. 6.1.5. Aseptic meningitis Aseptic meningitis is uncommon in individuals with SLE (prevalence of 1.4 to 1.6 %) and clinically manifests with headache, altered mental status, and signs of meningeal irritation, with or without fever. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis typically reveals lymphocytic pleocytosis and elevated protein levels. Imaging studies may demonstrate leptomeningeal enhancement [ – ]. Aseptic meningitis in pSD has similar clinical features to idiopathic presentation. The frequency of aseptic meningitis is difficult to be determined, since majority of publications are case reports or cases series [ ]. One cohort study reported a prevalence of 1.1 % [ ]. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis reveals leukocytosis (ranging from 33 to 900 cells/μL), with variable neutrophilic or lymphocytic predominance, elevated protein levels, and an elevated IgG index. The pathophysiology of aseptic meningitis is not fully elucidated in pSD, although there are theories that suggest it may be related to systemic inflammation.
